utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. The Chamber has considered how we would proceed with the present witness. He has to leave Thursday morning. We inquired with the parties whether there would be any possibility to continue this afternoon. That seems, and the Chamber accepts that, also in view of the limited time for preparation and the late disclosure of several documents that it would not be a good idea to try to force the Defence into this afternoon's session. Therefore, most likely, after the Defence has started cross-examination of this witness, we'll stop then, and the witness will then be recalled at a later stage. The Chamber always tries to avoid this, but under the present circumstances, there seems to be no alternative. Then, I also inform the parties that next Tuesday we'll have a late start in Court. That means that we'll start at approximately 11.00. So we'll miss the first session of one hour and a half and then have with one break another session. Then, Mr. Harmon, are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Good morning. Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just mention one thing, Your Honour. We are grateful for the Chamber not pushing us on this afternoon. That would have been unrealistic and we appreciate that. Your Honour, may I just mention that there was the question of the missing CD. Your Honour remembered that there was a problem. We delivered a CD to the UN DU. Just so that Your Honour and everybody knows what happened, it just -- most unfortunately, it appears got lost, went astray, for purely physical, practical reasons. It fell off some sort of trolley or truck or something like that. It picked the wrong time to do it. But I have -- the superintendent of the Detention Unit yesterday invited me to go and have a word. He explained to me what happened, and it was accompanied by a gracious apology in the circumstances because it shouldn't have happened. It is all now resolved, and it's not the sort of thing which is likely to be repeated. It was an entirely accidental matter, and it has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to hear it was accidental and not systematical error. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for Your Honours' attention, we'll be referring to 31052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it may be unnecessary, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with the binder of intercepts, and I will proceed. The usher could assist Mr. Kljuic, we will be referring to Tab 31052, intercept of the 13th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as soon as you've oriented yourself, please tell Mr. Harmon so that he will start your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, this is an intercept of the 13th of February 1992. The parties identified are Lukic and Radovan Karadzic. First of all, very briefly, can you tell us who Lukic is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a legal expert who took part in the SDS team in international negotiations on the establishment of the system in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention and the Court's attention to a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the English version, it's on page 1. It is toward the second Karadzic from the bottom. And let me quote Mr. Karadzic to you, Mr. Kljuic. "They want to bring our price down as much as possible so they can achieve success, to bring their price down and so as to achieve success. However, we cannot make concessions. We said we had made as many concessions as we could make. Our optimum is a Greater Serbia, and if not that, then a federal Yugoslavia. If not, and this is the only thing, there are no further concessions." Can you comment on that particular passage by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's quite clear. In keeping with their public proclamations and secret statements and projects, they weren't interested in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an independent one, a sovereign one with all three ethnic groups on a footing of equality and all citizens being equal. They had the project of a Greater Serbia. And failing, that then a federal Yugoslavia. However, as this was a conversation after Slovenia and Croatia had seceded, that is to say there was no federal Yugoslavia in the way it was in 1995 to 1990, but a federal Yugoslavia, a rump Yugoslavia, with Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro, and Macedonia left. And in that way, the non-Serb people would have absolutely no chance of existing. So here we have three points clearly expressed here. The first is a Greater Serbia; the second is a federal Yugoslavia without Croatia and Slovenia; and the third, what they actually did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the very clarity of those points as expressed in this transcript which raises the question of largely in these areas why this -- these matters are being explored with this witness at all. 90 per cent of the answer that he gave there is either absolutely well known or is absolutely obvious from the transcript. So it might be that we will get through this whole area more efficiently if we actually focus, and the questions might focus on that, on what this witness can actually add from his personal knowledge that we can't simply get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could proceed uninterrupted in this examination, I can conclude within the time period. It's up to me, Your Honour, to identify what parts of the intercepts I think are important and ask the questions in the way I deem them appropriate. Unless there is an objection. And I find this objection unreasonable. I think it is time consuming, and I would ask to be permitted to conduct the examination in the manner that I think is appropriate and has been conducted appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, there's some merit in what Mr. Stewart says, and at the same time I leave it to you to examine the witness as you wish. But please keep in mind that to hear the witness tell us what is already in the text of the intercept does not under all circumstances add very much to what the Chamber should know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct your attention, Mr. Kljuic, to another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is found on page 3 of the English text. It is -- it starts from the bottom, the fourth Karadzic from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me read this portion to you: "And the professor has just seen the paper you delivered there" -- I'm sorry. Let me start again. This is Lukic. Lukic: And the professor has just seen the paper you delivered there, and he's not very happy with the fact that Bosnia and its present borders is being presented upon." Karadzic: No, I want to -- we may have perhaps a little -- Lukic: Well, he thinks that perhaps that should have been passed over in silence. But there you are. Karadzic: That's right. He's quite right. He's quite right because we might make some changes with the Croats. Lukic: Yes, yes. Karadzic: That's correct. That's correct. I thought we should meet the general requirements. They keep asking us to -- Lukic: To preserve it? Karadzic: Yes, yes. Can you tell us on the 13th of February in respect of the passage "we might make some changes with the Croats," can you expand on your understanding of that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they didn't wish to have a Bosnia-Herzegovina within its borders and frameworks as Lukic says here, "then we will preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina" or something, they tried in different ways to find partners for the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And one of the ways of doing that was to achieve a historical agreement with the representatives of the Muslims. However, they did that with politicians who did not have the mandate to represent their nation, that ethnic group, and so the attempt proved abortive. Karadzic and his men tried for days to talk to me and establish contacts of that kind; that is to say, to shatter Bosnia-Herzegovina in that way. When they failed with me, they were to do so with other Croat representatives, especially since on the 2nd of February 1992, I handed in my resignation to the post of president of the HDZ precisely because of the rifts in the party with respect to the policy to be waged in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I was the forerunner of the legal stance for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina whereas there were others who wanted Western Herzegovina to secede. And so before that and after that, there were to be agreements between Boban and Karadzic and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, who is Boban that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legitimately speaking, Boban was my vice-president in the party and representative in parliament in legal terms. But because of his close ties with Zagreb and the change in Zagreb's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, he in fact represented a strong separatist stream within the HDZ which considered that Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be preserved as a state, but rather that a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the native village of Mr. Boban himself, should be attached to the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can turn to the next intercept. It is at -- there's the KID number 31205. It's dated the 21st of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please let us know, Mr. Kljuic, once you've acquainted yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, there's a reference on the first page of the intercept "headquarters in Vraca." First of all, can you tell us where Vraca is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in -- on the fringes of the town, on the left bank of the Miljacka River, but very close to the inner city, the centre of town. It's just a five-minutes walk to Marin Dvor. And it's that part of town where it was well-known there was a police training school there during the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to two passages. The first is on page 1 of the English translation, towards the bottom. Momcilo Krajisnik: This is Momcilo Krajisnik here. What's going on down there? Radomir Ninkovic: Well, Karisik would explain what's going on better -- or this, hmm. On the next page of the intercept, we have a passage toward the top of page 2 of the English. Momcilo Krajisnik: Tell me, what's the situation like down there? I'm here. There's chaos there. Milenko Karisik: "Well, there's a lot of shooting down there. The members of the TO are engaged." First of all, do you know who Mr. Karisik is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karisik is mentioned quite a lot as being one of the policemen before the war and afterwards. I don't know what post he held in actual fact in the Serb police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, Mr. Kljuic, on the 21st of April, what was happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the police school was also a strategic point because it is at an elevation from which you can control quite a lot of the town. And in that school, there were all the children attending that school, the young people attending the school, and they took the children into custody and took them off to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there fighting in Sarajevo on the 21st of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every day, but there was still sporadic -- there were still sporadic gunfire. It wasn't a full-fledged conflict. That was to begin on the 2nd of May. But there was fighting in the streets in different parts of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the next intercept, which will be KID Number 31422. It is dated the 27th of May 1992, conversation with General Boskovic and an unknown general.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know General Boskovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For many years, quite by chance, from 1960 to 1964 we happened to be neighbours, lived next to one another. And then in 1992, we met up again because he came as a special -- anyway, he came from Belgrade, and I was a Presidency member. And throughout the month of May, I was engaged in negotiations under the sponsorship of UNPROFOR and General MacKenzie, that is to say, there were negotiations between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb rebels and the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army. And the subject they were discussing was the evacuation of the soldiers from the barracks. There were a number of those, and they had quite a lot of weapons. Those negotiations lasted for quite a long time. They were not successful. And then Milosevic decided to send General Boskovic from Belgrade. Before that, there was General Aksentijevic and some others, Simonovic. But then General Boskovic arrived on the scene to negotiate about the soldiers. And then they asked to take the weapons and materiel out of the barracks. We didn't allow them to do, that but we did allow the soldiers to leave the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To orient everybody in terms of this particular intercept, on page 1 of the English translation, it says, and I quote: "(General Boskovic is on the phone.)" And then Boskovic says: Boskovic: Hello. Unknown person, male person 1: Hello, General. Boskovic: Hello. Unknown male person: You're on the line. Karadzic is also with the general. So we have a conversation taking place with General Boskovic who was in the Sarajevo -- in Sarajevo, and we have a conversation with -- the other party is a general who is present with Karadzic. Is that the correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but neither you nor I know who that other general is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. Now if I could turn your attention to page 2 of the English translation, I will read part of this intercept. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Unknown male person: Yes, Nidjo. Boskovic: I've just arrived, Cadjo. Jankovic and I have just come back from the negotiations. Well, they haven't changed their opinion, and half of the weapons according to their specifications, has to, they said, to take these two barracks or keep all the weapons in the barracks and to relocate the barracks safely which they guarantee. Well, since General Mladic doesn't agree with the -- well, options -- Unknown male person: He can't. Mladic is not the boss there. Boskovic: Let me tell you -- Unknown male person: Call this one. Krajisnik. Boskovic: General, I'm coming to see you now, now when -- Unknown male person: Yes. Boskovic: I'm coming up there, and I'll tell you about it... So Krajisnik also stuck to his version last time. He won't give in. Not to give them a single tank any more. Unknown male person 1: Then do it this way. Boskovic: Yes. Unknown male person 1: If Krajisnik doesn't agree, then Mladic won't agree, and nobody will want to sign these contracts, agreements that we have signed. Boskovic: Yes. Unknown male person: Then what have we got left? Boskovic: They tell us... Unknown person 1: To tell the parents we are not able to take the children out of there." Can you -- I'd like to focus your observations on what this intercept says about the authority and the power of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, two matters are at stake here. First there's Milosevic's interest in Belgrade to have the soldiers taken out of the barracks, and then there is the interest of Krajisnik and Mladic, which is not to have JNA weapons left in the barracks for the local people. As I was involved in those negotiations on a daily basis, we quite simply requested that the soldiers be allowed to leave in safety and that they leave us half of the weapons because it was a joint army. When they said that half of the weapons should be given to us, they said that half should be given to the Serbian forces, too. This is something they did not accept. General Boskovic came on behalf of Milosevic from Belgrade and his primary task was to save the soldiers. He wasn't at all interested in whom the weapons would be given to. He generously said "You take it, or the Bosnians take it. Give me the soldiers." However, in Lukavica, which is where the military headquarters was located at the time, he wasn't able to obtain the support of General Mladic. As to the seriousness of the situation, this can be shown by the fact that General Boskovic was left in the Presidency where I was. He couldn't go to sleep over in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kljuic, what does this say or suggest in respect of Mr. Krajisnik's authority in the absence of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's certain that Karadzic transferred that authority to Mr. Krajisnik because that's how it was set up in terms of the establishment. But Mr. Krajisnik, I must say, did not take part in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn to another intercept, then, it will be the intercept found at KID tab 31425 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask for a clarification, Mr. Harmon. If you look at the first page of the intercept we just saw, I think you told us that Karadzic was with the unknown male person. Is that the correct understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it says in the intercept here, as Mr. Harmon said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then may I ask you, where the unknown male person says "You're on the line. Karadzic is also with the General," well, we know that two generals are having this conversation. Wouldn't it be true that if someone is with me, that one would say "you're on the line. Karadzic is also with me," instead of "with the General"? Apart from several generals being involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we comment, this transcript does look a little bit disconcerting. The fact -- I appreciate Your Honour's questions, and the same questions arise. We've got the in brackets General Boskovic is on the phone, and then not in brackets we've got this passage Karadzic is also with the general. It does at least seem to be some serious doubt as to whether this does accurately set out the content of the conversation. This could be an example of where we really ought to play this particular intercept to get it straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your suggestion is to play this intercept because it raises some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than happy to do that. I would have to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's continue at this moment, and we'll come back to that. And you're aware that there are some questions in relation to who actually is speaking, whether it's just one male person or more male persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can first of all get through the remainder of these intercepts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, when I come with it at a later stage, you might not be prepared to have it played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next intercept. We'll clarify where Mr. Karadzic is in a few minutes, Mr. Kljuic. Let's go to the next intercept, and that is 31425. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is dated the 27th of May 1992. It's a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Radivoje Grkovic. There are only two small passages I want to refer you to, Mr. Kljuic. The first is found on page 1 toward the top of the English translation. Of course, we'll start at the top. Grkovic: Yes. Unidentified female: Hello. Grkovic: Yes. Unidentified female: Is this Nedzarici? Grkovic: Yes. What can I do for you? Unidentified female: Good evening. I'm calling from Mr. Krajisnik's office. Could you hold the line please. Excuse me, who am I talking to? Grkovic: You're talking to Grkovic, Nedzarici battalion commander. And then if we turn to page 2 of the English translation, I'll read you a related passage. Krajisnik: Good evening. Grkovic: How are you, Mr. President? Krajisnik: I'm well. Who is this? Grkovic: It's Radivoje Grkovic, Nedzarici Battalion commander. Krajisnik: Listen, Grkovic. Grkovic: Yes? What's the situation in Halilovici? Can you give a -- Grkovic: You know what, I cannot give much information on the phone. It's being tapped. Krajisnik: I know. Tell me. Grkovic: The latest information I have from the brigade command is that 66 vehicles -- Krajisnik: Is the barracks under attack? Grkovic: That barracks was to be evacuated tonight. Unfortunately it was to be today but -- Krajisnik: Evacuated? But is it under attack? Grkovic: At the moment, no. It's not under attack. Krajisnik: Come again? Grkovic: It's not under attack. Krajisnik: It's not? Grkovic: Who would attack it now when it's empty? Krajisnik: It's not empty. Grkovic: What do you mean it's not empty? Krajisnik: There's lots of artillery left there and other stuff. Grkovic: Well, I was in contact with their commander every day. Krajisnik: Okay. Let me tell you. And that's where I will end my reading. What does this intercept -- first of all, Nedzarici, is that in metropolitan Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's in the centre of the new part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when there's a reference to Halilovici, is that in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's from Nedzarici to the right. That's where a barracks was located. That's an area that is also very near to Nedzarici. But it's about 1 kilometre away, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in respect of this intercept, I'd like you to comment on the ability of Mr. Krajisnik to be informed of the situation on the ground. Can you give us your observations on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite clearly, the gentleman was asking for information from the field, and the barracks -- the soldiers were removed from the barracks as agreed by the commissions under General MacKenzie. Whereas Belgrade tried to save the people through General Boskovic, the local people, the local Serbs, especially the lower-ranking officers, didn't allow them to leave the barracks without the weapons and for the weapons to be left for the Territorial Defence. This was in their interest because if they assumed that if the Territorial Defence obtained the weapons, the balance of the combat forces in the field would change. That meant that the strength of the Territorial Defence would be increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to another intercept then, Mr. Kljuic. It's found at KID 30289, and it is an intercept of July the 8th, 1991. It should be approximately six tabs, 30289. It would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, it's the sixth one. The sixth tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The sixth tab from the one that we were on. I'll be directing Your Honours' attention at the passages of the first three speakers of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find it, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you the first passages of this intercept, because that's where I want to direct your attention, Mr. Kljuic. Starting at the top, this is a conversation on July the 8th 1991 between Karadzic and Vitomir Zepinic. Radovan Karadzic: ... meet every morning and have it sorted out. I was with Izetbegovic and Zulfikarpasic last night, and I told them openly we would form a parallel government. We would form a parallel police. If they exclude our people and government, then they will still have to pay for them. We would exclude all our people who are armed. We would form completely a parallel state if you continue to fuck us around. And he only stated -- stared at me and winked because he knew that we would do it. God could not stop us in that because they started to fuck around with us, and there is no doubt their -- we would do it in a week. So let there be war so we'll have it finished once. Zepinic: There's no words that follow that particular block. And then Karadzic says: Karadzic: We'll finish it once... Us on small con... We are now before signing a very important document with them, with Muslims. But I will not sign it before these things, these things are finished. It's horrible. I will go to Devedlaka now to make sure that no one will ever dare to propose something privately that is not verified in the party. Now, can you give us your observations about these particular comments by Mr. Karadzic. And this is July, again, of 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a period during which there weren't any incidents in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. But in Croatia, war was raging, and there were many victims. That was the time when -- that was an occasion when Karadzic first attempted to reach an agreement with the Muslims. He wanted to withdraw them from the block of those fighting for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. He wanted to reach a separate agreement, a historical agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims. And by doing this, regardless of the fact that they denied this, they would have been against the Croats. Because if they had unified, if they had united on a political level, the Muslims and the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in such a case the Croats would have had no possibility of surviving, naturally. Uniting in such a manner and that historical agreement meant that the Croats would be given a province, the province of Western Herzegovina which would be annexed to Croatia. And this is something that they had been preparing for a long time. There were the discussions with Zulfikarpasic. Apart from that, they also spoke to Izetbegovic and suggested he be the president of the assembly in the rump Yugoslavia because Karadzic wanted to break up a unified defence mechanism in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. It is quite clear that they did not want a Bosnia and Herzegovina which would be organised on democratic principles. We were always in favour of a Belgian or a Swiss system. However, when Izetbegovic didn't agree to this, he got involved with someone else called Zulfikarpasic. But he had no political influence and wasn't respected by the Muslims and as a result was not able to carry out that task. So while war was being waged in Croatia, they observed what was happening in Croatia and in a certain sense threatened the Muslims and said this will happen to you, too, so let's try and reach a historical agreement to help you avoid such a situation. And all negotiations were accompanied by Karadzic's ultimatums, and that can be seen from this part of the discussion because he said "we'll make our own state, our own police force, our own army," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also in this particular first passage says, "Let there be war so we'll have it finished once." You mentioned in your testimony on Monday that there was always a threat that was coming to you and to the Bosniaks in respect of war. This is consistent with that approach that you described on Monday, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they never suggested a suggestion on what the democratic the Bosnia-Herzegovina should look like. They would only appear in these discussions, but they never really accepted to discuss matters of common concern. All they did was say that there would be a war, and they were quite aware of the fact that they were going into a war. Since they had the force and the support of Mr. Milosevic, they were quite certain that they would win the war. But they could never win the war. They could commit crimes. They could take territory. They could expel people. They could destroy property. And they did destroy towns. You know, in Sarajevo, they even shelled maternity wards and nursery schools. They could do all that, but they couldn't destroy the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's a historical entity that has suffered, but it will survive. That's for sure. And it will be a multi-ethnic state because that's a modus vivendi in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of this, however, demonstrates they did not want discussions that would be based on the way the institutions within the system functioned, and that would be based -- or that would strive to develop legal norms for the joint life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next intercept. It's at 305, tab 77. It should be the next intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's the intercept, Counsel, September the 3rd, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond 1991, a conversation between Deronjic and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you, in view of the last answer, it goes very much through general programme statements rather than an explanation of what the exhibit says. So would you please keep a bit more control over --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I don't know whether it's -- the next one ends with 511 and not 577.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I haven illegible tab number written on mine. That's why I tried to identify it as the intercept of September 3rd, 1991, the conversation between Karadzic and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last three digits being 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The transcript has it September the 3rd, but I think Mr. Harmon said 23rd quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to a passage in this, Mr. Kljuic, that's found on page 1 of the intercept toward the middle of the English version. It starts with Mr. Krajisnik saying: Krajisnik: What's up? Karadzic: Well, our people are incapable of doing anything. Hmm, Alija is trying to mobilise... to create an army through expansion... the unlimited expansion of part of the reserve force. Krajisnik: Protection, right? Karadzic: Mobilising the reserve force. We would have to call him urgently, urgently, hmm, the two of us to sit down with him and tell him that's -- that that's civil war. Now, I want to be very precise in this question. Can you tell me, Mr. Kljuic, what does this suggest in relation to the relationship, the collaborative relationship between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, a subject about which you testified on Monday?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear that they had positions that they shared contact on a daily basis. That's not at all unusual. But it doesn't say that they were mobilising the reserve police force here. After the JNA had taken the weapons of the Territorial Defence, the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina was only left with the possibility of mobilising 60.000 reserve policemen. That would have meant that the Croats and Muslims together would have 40.000 guns and the Serbs would have had 20.000 guns. That was the balance of power in the field. If there were 60.000 guns, then the territory couldn't have been taken in such a way. This was the only possibility of resisting the aggression. However, sabotage was committed on the 30th of March. That police force was disbanded. It's obvious that Karadzic and Krajisnik were afraid of the reserve police force being mobilised because they would have resisted the aggression and diminished their chances of carrying out a rapid strike in a vast stretch of land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next intercept, it's 30630. It's the very next intercept, Mr. Kljuic, in your binder. This is a conversation of the 13th of October 1991, the conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Momo. And in this intercept, I believe you have identified the voice of Momo as Momo, Momcilo Mandic. Let me read then --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who Mr. Mandic was.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandic was one of the leaders of the joint police force in the prewar Bosnia-Herzegovina. And during the war, he occupied the post of minister of justice I believe or something similar in the Government of Republika Srpska. But as he's a professional policeman, he was always involved in all police operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me read a passage that's found on page 2 of the English translation, and I will read starting from a part of what Radovan Karadzic says. I'll be reading mid-passage. Karadzic: ... because that is a mechanism which was used to manipulate us and the Serb members of parliament are fed up with all those attempts to proclaim independence. Alija Izetbegovic admitted to us... Mandic: I heard. Karadzic: ... that this sovereignty means independence. Mandic: Yes. Karadzic: And that is the way Croatia took, and we know what is going to happen here. That has nothing to do with Karadzic's or anyone else's decision. We know exactly what is going to happen. There is no -- Mandic: Definitely. That is clear to the people in Belgrade. Karadzic: In just a couple of days, Sarajevo will be gone, and there would be 500.000 dead. In one month, Muslims be annihilated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Numbers of Serbs will be reduced, and Croats will be the only ones to profit because they will keep their municipalities. This is on the 13th of October 1991. Can you -- and this was shortly before, was it not, the speech that we saw a video clip of when Mr. Karadzic in the parliament said that the Bosnian nation would disappear? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the evil that was done, this is very early. And this speaks to the fact that this obsession with an aggression that they would destroy, kill, devastate is a sick idea. And I must say that Karadzic -- well, let me say that this was an intercept, but he did exploit this kind of thing a great deal, especially when speaking tete-a-tete. He would say, "We'll destroy you, we'll kill you." And all this was geared towards instilling fear because, you see, he says if they will take the road that Croatia took and this other man says "Well, the people in Belgrade know what that means." So I would impress upon you one point all the time, that what was done in Bosnia was no new idea, nor is it a separate programme. It is just part of the general programme in Milosevic's plan which was encoded and encrypted under the name of RAM, R-A-M. So you can imagine how the negotiations were conducted, faced with the situation in which Karadzic and the Serb leadership behaved in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next intercept, Mr. Kljuic. It is found -- should be found three tabs down. It is intercept 31086. It is dated March 1st, 1992. It's a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Rajko Djukic. It's a very short intercept. Just cast your eye on it. Let me direct your attention to a passage on -- it's found on page 1 of the English. It's Radovan Karadzic, toward the bottom, Your Honours. Radovan Karadzic: Get them. Get them to rise up and have things prepared. They should close everything tonight. Djukic: Erm... Karadzic: All the exits. Djukic: There is no other way, my friend. Karadzic: Have them close all the exits. Very, very briefly, Mr. Kljuic, can you tell us what this intercept -- what these people are talking about.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Djukic was a high-ranking functionary of the SDS. And during this period of time, he was in charge of the blockades. On two of the occasions, they blocked Sarajevo, and their aim was to see whether they could cut across the town. You will remember that I mentioned a part of town called Pofalici, and that was a strategically very important because, the most important strategy point because if they cut us off there, the old town, all the institutions and organisational systems, would be left isolated. So when Karadzic says that all exits and entrances into town should be closed, then that is tantamount to a threat because Sarajevo is a city in a valley, situated in a valley, in a depression. And when you close off the approaches into town and the entrances and exits, then the danger is that there will be no food, no water. And that was supposed to be a psychological shock in the form of a barter so that they give up in the negotiations the idea of independence. And it was done on the very day that the results of the referendum were made public. So this was Karadzic's response to the 64 per cent or more of the citizens' votes in favour of independence. This process was to be repeated over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to another intercept, Mr. Kljuic. It is an intercept with the KID ID number of 31208, a conversation between Vojislav Seselj and Branislav Gavrilovic in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you identify Vojislav Seselj for the record, who he is and what role he had in the events in Bosnia. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojislav Seselj was a Communist Youths member and he had political problems in Sarajevo. He was even arrested on one occasion, and then he went to Belgrade where he became one of the leading nationalists. He absolutely denied the right of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to a state of their own. He was the president of the radical party, and I think he still is today. And he had many paramilitary formations which he sent to the battlefield in Bosnia, and more especially to Sarajevo. And the greatest crimes in Sarajevo were committed by the so-called "White Eagles."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the White Eagles his particular paramilitary formation? Or do you know what relationship he had to the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, at that time, four paramilitary formations were most noticeable. There was a certain Jovic, there was Arkan, there was Seselj, and there was Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me read this passage of the intercept. I'm mistaken. I gave you the -- I asked you a question, and my information that was the basis of that question was incorrect. So let me ask you this question: In respect of this intercept, I will read from the bottom of the page. Seselj: Look, I have just called Pale. I can't find Radovan, and nobody can find him. Radoslav Gavrilovic: Yeah. Seselj: But I have left a message that if they don't get our men out, we'll withdraw our men from the front lines, and we'll never deploy them again. Gavrilovic: All right. Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously out of all the paramilitary formations, Seselj had the largest number. However, this is one of his groups which had entered the centre of town and was probably in the encirclement. And as far as Karadzic is concerned and his relationship towards Seselj, he was not sincere. Karadzic was just interested in Seselj to the extent to which he was able to supply paramilitaries to commit crimes. So from this dialogue, we can see that Karadzic in fact didn't mind too much about Seselj's people who was surrounded and in an encirclement, but Seselj for his part put an ultimatum. So they were heterogenous, in actual fact. But they were together working on this project, and we can even say they were some sort of rivals, they were rivals of sorts, because both men had pretensions of being the overall Serb leaders. Karadzic thought once the job was done and once all Serb lands were united, that he would be the one who had united them and not Milosevic. And his ambitions were to be the leader of all Serbs in the former Yugoslavia. So Seselj says here unless you save my men, I'm not going to supply you with any more soldiers. So that would be a great handicap and drawback to Karadzic and his policy he wanted to further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll proceed with KID number 31272. It's two tabs later. It's an intercept of the 5th of May 1992, and it is a conversation between many, many people, including Momo Mandic, Brane Kvesic, Bruno Stojic and Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kvesic. Thank you. Can you take a look at this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already read the document. I know all the people concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then direct your attention, Mr. Kljuic, to certain passages in this intercept. We can turn to, Your Honours, page 4 of the English translation. This is a conversation between Kvesic and Mandic. First of all, can you identify who Mr. Kvesic is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic was the head of the Bosnian Herzegovinian intelligence service. That is to say, he was one of the assistants to the minister of the interior. He was a Croat from Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- this is Kvesic: Kvesic: So you are right there in Pale, are you? Mandic: Well, we are not. We came down to the city. Kvesic: Yes, yes. Mandic: We came down and cleaned Grbavica... Kvesic: Is that so? Mandic: ...There, we hold Ilidza, Dobrinja and Nedzarici all the way to the student campus and so on. Kvesic: Please tell me the number of dead. They said something about it on the television. Are those lies or... Does this describe fighting in Sarajevo, Mr. Kljuic? This is the 5th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And already then Mandic is reporting and saying that Grbavica is being cleared and the greatest crime was committed at Grbavica which was otherwise an multiethnic settlement. But when they took control of the school at Vraca which we mentioned a moment ago, the police school when they took that over, then they were able to control the entire terrain from a centrally located bridge. And it's a very densely populated area, and when he says -- when Momo Mandic says that they have cleaned Grbavica, that means that they have -- that they took away many people. Some they killed. Some went in for an exchange. So that Grbavica already at that period of time, when this conversation took place in May, actually it had already been ethnically cleaned, cleansed. And he is bragging to Kvesic about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 5 of the English translation, toward the bottom, Your Honours. There's a colloquy between Mandic and Kvesic. Mandic says: M: Well, we are holding the Turks under siege. We'll starve them a bit, you know. Kvesic: Are you? Mandic: And then we'll give them everything from the Eternal Flame to Vratnik. Everything up there. And then both of them are laughing. Very briefly, can you interpret that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all normal people reading this conversation, they will be struck by the brutality of this conversation, in view of the fact that these were highly placed policemen in Bosnia and Herzegovina speaking. The identification of our Muslims and equating them to Turks, referring to them as Turks, was part of Serb propaganda. And you'll see on one of the pictures Mladic entering Srebrenica, and he says, "We have taken our revenge on the Turks." However, at that time in Sarajevo, there were over 150.000 citizens who were not Muslims. On the other hand, they say that they will give us the area from the Eternal Flame to Vratnik, which is just the old part of town, exclusively the old part of town. And I must say I'm very proud of that part of town because per square kilometre you have two Orthodox churches, five mosques, two Catholic churches, and one synagogue. So that is the nucleus, the centre of the multi-ethnic city of Sarajevo. It is 500 years old, and they say -- they tell us that they're going to leave us that and then start laughing arrogantly. Now, if you just look at the conversation without knowing who the people speaking are, you can imagine what the project itself was like and Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond who the protagonists of the project are, who put it into practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to page 7, starting at the top. This is a conversation between Momcilo Mandic and Bruno Stojic. First of all, can you identify Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bruno Stojic was one of the assistants to the minister of the interior. For all intents and purposes, he was head of the financial department of the police force. Later on, he was to become the minister of defence of the so-called Herceg Bosna state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian Croat, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian Croat, like Kvesic, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read the passage: Mandic: Hi. Stojic: Where have you been, my Serb brother? Mandic: Where have you been, my free Croat brother? Then there's laughter. Stojic: What is this that you are doing, you motherfucker? Mandic: We want to build a new and nice Sarajevo. Stojic: New and nice Sarajevo? Mandic: Yes. We don't like this old synagogues and mosques. We have to change architecture and everything. Your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all those who wished to learn the truth, this statement is perhaps sufficient, the one made by Momo Mandic, to illustrate the essence of that Fascism, the kind that wanted to change the architecture of Sarajevo. The architecture of Sarajevo -- and I explained it a moment ago -- what you will find on just one square metre of the centre of town cannot be changed because it is made up of the structure of people. You can harm it, you can devastate it, but you cannot eliminate all the factors that make up Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina for good. However, the brutality and the simplifications that took place in putting into effect the programme that Mandic is bragging about, is boasting of, speak of the lowest type of mental makeup of the people in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I invited you to keep control over the witness answering the question instead of making these kind of statements. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me direct your attention to another portion of this intercept. It's found on page 10 of the English version, three lines up from the bottom. This is a continuing conversation between Stojic and Mandic. And Mandic says, and I quote: "We don't want the Neretva, we want the left bank of the Neretva." Now, this is the 5th of May, and we saw in Exhibit 47 the strategic objectives of the Serbian people that were announced in the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May. You testified that the strategic objectives were not an epiphany on the 12th of May, that they were known in advance of the 12th of May. Does this confirm, this comment by Mr. Mandic confirm your previous testimony in that respect?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic exactly confirms the borders envisaged for a Greater Serbia, referring to the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to, then, two passages, additional passages. Again, this is actually a new conversation -- new conversants. This is Bruno Stojic and Mico Stanisic. First of all, can you identify Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is on page 13. I'm going to be referring to two parts of this, Your Honour. They will be found at about halfway through on page 13 of the English and the top of page 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify Mr. Stanisic, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is also a prewar high-ranking police officer, and before the war he had a leading police role at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Referring to page 13 of the English, Mico Stanisic: Stanisic: Hello. Stojic: Where are you, Minister? Stanisic: Where are you, man, what are you doing? Stojic: What is this? Are you out of your fucking minds? Stanisic: Well, fuck, what can you do? Stojic: How can you fight us, man? Stanisic: Fight who? Stojic: Well, us here, what's wrong with you? Stanisic: We are not fighting you. Stojic: You are. Not you and Momo, but Karadzic and the rest are fighting us. Stanisic: Come on, man, let's sit down and make an agreement. And then if we go over to page 15 at the top of the English translation, the conversation which continues, Stanisic said: Stanisic: "We'll give you all this that is here, Visoko, Vares, Kakanj." Stojic: Who are you giving us anything? Stanisic: We'll give you also Zenica. Stojic: Let me tell, you, man. Stanisic: Well give you fucking Zenica too. Stojic: That is the autonomous Banovina of Croatia of 1939. We need what is ours. Don't fucking give us that. Can you give us your comments on this conversation that relate to a solicitation to make an agreement.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, from this conversation, you can see apart from the fact that they're boasting, that is to say Stanisic and Mandic, about what they had done in Sarajevo, that Bruno Stojic as more serious than Brane Kvesic is criticising them for the fighting that is going on in Herzegovina, and you have to know that at the time the JNA was in control of Mostar, and that they had this General Perisic there, and that they shot at the Croatian lands. Apart from the stories about Neretva and the border that the Serbs were putting forward as proposals not being accepted by these two Croats, there's this conversation now as to why you're shooting at us, as they say. Bruno Stojic is asking "why are you shooting at us?" Because we're not fighting you, because it was only the Muslims or Territorial Defence which was multi-ethnic at the time that was engaged in the fighting. And since they did not have the necessary competence, these two high-ranking Serb policemen, in fact, wanted to strike an agreement or to have an agreement between the Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats so as to be able to focus on Sarajevo. Excuse me. On that occasion, Bruno Stojic is putting forward Croatia's demands dating back to 1939 which was the Banovina of Croatia, which was an administrative division within the frameworks of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia which never came into effect and was never really implemented, in reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kljuic. We have the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We could play that now, Your Honour. I see from the transcript it's a short transcript. I can't tell you how long the intercept itself is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's KID 31423?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the one about which questions were raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, of course, we do not know how much time this will take. Would you have -- how much time would you need after we've clarified this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then I'm finished. I have to tender some exhibits that weren't tendered yesterday and I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No further questions. Then it might be wise to finish this before our first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I mean, if it generates some issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course, we would have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just coordinate this to make sure the intercept is ready. Your Honour, the intercept about which there are questions is 31422. If I said 31423. I see that both you and said 23, and it should be for the record 31422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were all of the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My questions are about...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The issue of General Boskovic and where Karadzic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's 422, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can play that now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I made the mistake, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unknown male person 1: Yes. Unknown male person 2: Hello. Unknown male person 1: Hey, Nidjo. Pardon? Unknown male person 1: Is Nidjo there. Unknown male person 2: Yes, he is. Unknown male person 1: Your boss wants to speak to him. Unknown male person 2: That's why I'm calling. Unknown male person 1: Okay, put him through. Unknown male person 2: Here you are. Boskovic: Hello. Unknown male person 1: Hello, General. Boskovic: Hello. Unknown male person 1: You're on the line. Karadzic is also with the General. Boskovic: Uh-huh. Unknown male person 1: You're on the line. Boskovic: Put the General on the line. Unknown male person 1: That one is not here, you know. Boskovic: No, I won't be long. Unknown male person 1: Okay. Boskovic: But he has to pick up the phone. Tell him to pick up the receiver. Unknown male person 1: Yes, yes. Boskovic: There you go. Unknown male person 1: Hello? Boskovic: Hey, General. Unknown male person 1: Yes, Nidjo. Boskovic: I've just arrived. Cadjo, Jankovic and I have come back from the negotiations. Well, they haven't changed their opinion and half of the weapons according to their specifications has to ... they said ... to take these two barracks or to keep all the weapons in the barracks and to relocate the barracks safely, which they guarantee. Well, since General Mladic doesn't agree with the... well, options. Unknown male person 1: He can't. Mladic not the boss there. Boskovic: Let me tell you... Unknown male person 1: Call this one... Krajisnik. Boskovic: General, I'm coming to see you now. Now, when it... Unknown male person 1: Yes? Boskovic: I'm coming up there and I'll tell you about it... So Krajisnik also stuck to his version last time. He won't give in, not to give them a single tank any more. Unknown male person 1: Then do it this way. Boskovic: Yes. Unknown male person 1: If Krajisnik doesn't agree, then Mladic won't agree and nobody will want to sign these agreements that we have signed. Boskovic: Yes. Unknown male person 1: Then what have we got left? Boskovic: They tell us ... Unknown male person 1: To tell the parents that we are not able to get the children out of there. Boskovic: Yes, I'll come there tonight, General, and we'll talk about it because they demand -- they say they are... that we are an equal partner... party in negotiations, and Republika Srpska isn't because they say that the army concluded this agreement and not the Republika Srpska... They say this... Unknown male person 1: Well, we... those are not their weapons, they're ours. Boskovic: Yes, but regarding the ... I mean the barracks, they say those are your units, your armed forces members. Unknown male person 1: Well, that's true, they're ours. That's correct. Boskovic: However, this... Mladic says that it's their territory now. He doesn't agree. He told me this morning that he would only settle for relocation. Unknown male person 1: Let me ask you once again. Will he give that half of the weapons down there or not? Boskovic: Okay. Unknown male person 1: If he won't, we are leaving the weapons to them and bailing the kids out of there. Boskovic: I see and I'll come to see him tonight. Unknown male person 1: Tell them so and you come here to make arrangements. Boskovic: Yes, yes. Unknown male person 1: You will go back if necessary. Boskovic: Yes, sir. Unknown male person 1: Izetbegovic has just called me. Boskovic: What did he say? Unknown male person 1: He says that you should stay until you finish the job. Boskovic: And then I get sacrificed. I'll be sacrificed if I have to be, but only for the truth, justice and honesty. I won't be sacrificed for slander, insults and intrigues. That's the point. Unknown male person 1: Then come over here. Boskovic: I'll come over there, General. Unknown male person 1: Okay, then. And you'll go back tomorrow if you have to. Boskovic: Okay, General. Unknown male person 1: Good-bye, then. Boskovic: Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you consider the possibility that the unknown person 1 is not the same on the bottom of page 1 and then the unknown male person appearing on the top of page 2? Because it becomes totally illogic if the person who says "hello," the fourth entry on page 2, would be the same person unknown male person as we find under bottom of the second half of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll listen to this very carefully. But I would consider there are a number of possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I'm just pointing at one. I only asked you to consider that, to see whether there was any...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some exhibits from yesterday that I would like to tender so the record is complete. We played a video clip of Mrs. Plavsic kissing Arkan. We would like that to be tender as an exhibit, given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P300.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we would tender a CD with all of the intercepts that are contained in this binder as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P292.A.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And yesterday, we tried valiantly to play the portion of the 34th Bosnian Serb Assembly session. I ended up reading a transcript from that session. I have the video, and I would like to tender that and the transcript from the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be marked Prosecution Exhibit Number P301. And the transcript P301.A.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that concludes, Your Honour, my...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes, Your Honour, my direct examination of Mr. Kljuic. Mr. Kljuic, thank you very much for your patience and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we are aware that you have to leave tomorrow morning. Through the Victims and Witness section, we also know that if need would be, and it's very likely that we might not finish today, that you would be willing to come back to The Hague to finish your examination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for making yourself available even beyond these few days. We'll now first have a break until 11.00, and then Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would like to you to start cross-examination. And then we'll see where we come. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was informed that in the B/C/S version of 31422, it appears that the -- there's a third unknown person which appears approximately at the place I indicated. There's one unknown person 1, there's an unknown person 2, but there's also an unknown person without a number which appears to be the general. So if this would assist you...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that we consider that Your Honour is 100 per cent right about that. Ms. Cmeric, of course, is really our reliable source on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It goes exactly with Your Honour's description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you're ready to start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kljuic to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if probably doesn't make the slightest difference to the witness as far as his plans are concerned, Your Honour indicated to him that we might not finish with him today. If it's at all helpful to the witness, he could be told that there is no prospect that we will finish with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he's aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, the counsel for the Defence. You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you were asked a number of questions, and you described in outline at least various contacts you had had with various individuals. First of all, Mr. Karadzic, or Dr. Radovan Karadzic. You said that you had known Dr. Karadzic for about 25 to 30 years. And then you said that at the time when political parties, national political parties came into being, "our contacts took place on almost on a daily basis until April 1992." Now, the time when political parties or national political parties came into being, we're talking about the middle or second half of 1990, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So through from 1990 until April 1992, that's the period in which you were saying you had contact with him almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that true of the early part of that period, so that for the second half of 1990 and early 1991, was the pattern of your meetings or contacts with Dr. Karadzic broadly the same as it was through the later period of second half of 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, we were on better terms because we all wanted the regime to be changed, and we wanted a democratic society to replace the communist one. However, as matters grew increasingly complex with regard to the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we continued to have frequent contact but we were on far more official terms. The relationship was far more official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's take that first phase, then, of the second half of 1990 and perhaps through to, say, April 1991. Let's take that period. What would -- at that time, what was the nature of your -- you used the word contacts as it came out in English. What's the nature of your contacts with Dr. Karadzic at that time? Type of contact, frequency of contact.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the period during the pre-election campaign. We had certain joint positions, all three nationalist parties had certain positions that they held in common. There was the issue of the elections, of how the elections would be conducted, et cetera. And there was even a dilemma as to how the people would be represented or how the peoples would be represented in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the socialist period, there were two Serbs, two Croats, and two Muslims in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there was one person who was a representative of other citizens who had identified themselves as Yugoslavs. All this had to do with certain ethnic minorities or people who did not have an ethnic identity of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, perhaps I can say that of course I don't suggest that the issues don't tie in with the question of the contacts and the meetings because clearly there is a point at which they do, but primarily I'm inviting you to describe the nature and frequency of contacts and give us only the minimum, please, of the underlying issues and background which assist an understanding of your answer to that question. So if we can focus, please, on my question which was the type and frequency of the contacts with Dr. Karadzic during that period.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The type of contact was very correct. We had a certain number of meetings because there were certain public discussions, et cetera. We had the number of meetings that was possible at the time. And we would meet as often as was necessary given the daily policies. If we had something that was a matter of common interest, then Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic and myself would see each other twice a day. If there was nothing we were at all interested in, then we wouldn't see each other so frequently. But after the elections in November 1990, because of the agreement about how to form government and how to represent the various peoples, we would have frequent working meetings. And as a result, we were more frequently in contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it's really -- what I'm trying to pin down really is that you were there, we weren't. Words like "frequent" and "as often as necessary," that's in a sense, that's the problem. I need you, please, to tell the Trial Chamber as clearly as you can what you mean by that. So over that -- let's forget about pre-election. Let's not worry too much about that. But post-November 1990 elections, say, for the next six months, let's take that time period. I'd like you to give the Trial Chamber a picture of over that period how often you saw Dr. Karadzic and what type of contact it was, whether it was casual in passing, whether it was one-to-one meetings, whether it was larger meetings. Just some clearer idea.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were official discussions between the leaders of three nationalist parties. These meetings took place very frequently. We also appeared together at certain public gatherings. We had some friends in common; for example, the lawyer, Dr. Karadzic. And we also had certain tete-a-tetes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you were specifically asked to specify words as "frequently." So you said "official discussions between the leaders of the parties. These meetings took place very frequently." Was that once a week, once a month, two times a day? Tell us how frequent on average.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least three times a week.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said meetings with the -- Mr. Karadzic's lawyers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This took place during the first six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were talking about -- I'm a bit confused now. If you say "official discussions," did you mean together with Mr. Karadzic's lawyers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I meant those lawyers, these were private meetings held in the -- there were dinners. They were such meetings. But when I say party meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as I said, two or three times a week for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the private meetings. Now the private meetings, such as dinners. How often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not very frequently, but Sarajevo is a small town. And at the time, it was not a problem to go to the main hotel and to meet there, not just Mr. Karadzic and myself. But this was the case for many people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. You say not very frequently. Once a month? Once every two months? On average.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first six months, it was very frequent. It was only when the war started in Croatia that relations cooled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was the first six months after the elections, private meetings such as dinners, how frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not that frequent. Perhaps once in a month or once every two weeks. But there were official discussions that took place quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the third category was just exchange of a few words in passing. How often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were -- these meetings were more frequent than the dinners that were had because Mr. Karadzic was also a literary man. We would meet at literary evenings and in the theatre. Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is about how frequent. Would that happen twice a week or once every two weeks or... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I couldn't say. Sometimes it was five times a week and sometimes it was only once a week, and sometimes not at all. It depended on the situation. But there's absolutely no doubt about the fact that it was frequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I went through this exercise also to make clear to you that careful listening to the question will give you a clue on what the answer should be about. It was the type of meetings. We've now identified three types -- If there's another one, please tell us -- and frequency. Not all the rest, maybe of great importance, but it was not asked to you at this moment. And if the backgrounds and whether Dr. Karadzic was a literary man or not is not at this moment the subject of the question. If Mr. Stewart would like to know that, he'll certainly ask you as one of his follow-up questions. May I invite you again to carefully listen what exactly the question is about. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Kljuic, may I simply once again observe that if you could please, please try to avoid using phrases like "frequent" or "very frequent" or "not very frequent" without any explanation because really that's what I'm asking you give precise information about. Can we take it that that last category, the meeting in the theatre or at some literary society and so on, that all those meetings would have been of a fairly incidental social nature. You might just say hello in passing or exchange some conversation about the time of day or something. Is that a fair summary of that category?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did mention a few minutes ago tete-a-tete meetings with Mr. Karadzic by which I understand you to mean meetings where it was just Mr. Karadzic and just you, or just the two of you. Is it correct that during -- let's take that same six-month period to start with, from November 1990 through to April 1991. Is it correct that you did have at least some such meetings with Mr. Karadzic where only the two of you were present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how -- as best you can do now, how many such meetings do you say that you had with Dr. Karadzic during that six-month period? Of course, I'm not asking you to be precise to the exact number, but how many do you say that you've had?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had four or five very open and confidential meetings at which only Mr. Karadzic and I were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you put as accurate a time as -- date as you can on what the first of those meetings would have been post-November 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one in December for sure. This had to do with our discussion on the idea of how to divide power. In order to understand the nature of this task, you should be aware of the fact that after the elections, three national parties --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, may I say straightaway and following exactly what His Honour said, I hope, if I then wish to ask you about the subject of the meeting -- well, I may very well do on occasion -- if I wish to ask you about the subject of the meeting, I will do that. If we take the questions in little bite-sized chunks, if I ask you the date of the meeting, that's what I wish you to answer. If I then want to know about the content of the meeting, I will ask you another question. If we follow that process as outlined by His Honour, we'll get on famously, Mr. Kljuic. So you had the first meeting with Dr. Karadzic. The question I want to ask you is this: Did you keep -- when you went to that meeting, for example, with Dr. Karadzic, did you keep a notebook? Did you make notes during the meeting? Did you keep any sort of agenda, diary, record of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't keep a diary. But I did take notes of a certain kind. I would record the positions of the SDS; that is to say, of Mr. Karadzic and the positions of the SDA, that is to say of Alija Izetbegovic because that was essential. So that at meetings of my party leadership, I could state what our partners wanted and what they demanded of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, thank you. I think we can see probably fairly straightforwardly what the purpose of keeping those notes would be. Did you keep those notes in a notebook of some sort?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wrote them down on sheets of paper that I had on me when I needed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll come on to subsequent meetings. But can we take it the four or five meetings that you had with Dr. Karadzic during that period, that every time you took notes in some form or another in the way that you've described?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retain those notes and do you retain those notes up to the present day?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm writing a book about Bosnia and I use a lot of documents, including the notes that I took at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they are physically in Sarajevo, are they, those notes, at the moment? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they're in my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
