utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, would you have any objection, first of all, to bringing such notes with you when you return to The Hague to give evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is my right as an author. These are my positions. And I'll be expressing what I wrote down in public. I wrote down what Karadzic said. I wrote down what he wanted. And then I relayed this information at an HDZ meeting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, at the moment I'm simply asking you that single question which you very helpfully answered that you don't object to bringing that material with you. A supplementary question in that area is: Would you have any objection if it can be arranged as a practical matter to forwarding through whatever channels are appropriate to The Hague in advance of your returning to The Hague, photocopies of any such notes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you haven't understood me correctly. I said that I wouldn't provide you with this. These are things that I want to have published in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that there was -- the question, I do agree with you, Mr. Stewart, the question was whether Mr. Kljuic would have any objection. And his answer was no. But from what follows, it appears that "no" rather stands for I'm not willing to bring it with me. And that's now confirmed by Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's clear now, Your Honour. I must say, I had not understood. I mean, it's just my misunderstanding. I had not understood the second half of the answer as contradicting. We see now that, apparently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can we get it clear. You are saying you do object, and if it's simply a voluntary matter, you're saying you will refuse to bring such material to The Hague with you, are you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I provide you with my notes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer my question, please, Mr. Kljuic. I want to get it clear. I'm not going to answer your questions, with respect. Answer my question, please. Is it that you are actually saying you will refuse, unless some compulsion is brought to bear, you will refuse to bring this material with you to The Hague, will you? Take a moment to think about it, Mr. Kljuic. I do wish to have your clear answer on this.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, these notes, which is the case for all the other documents, too, constitute material that I'm working with now that I'm writing my book. And I don't want to provide it to anyone before it's published. This is the right of every author. And in addition, I don't think that other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is clear, Mr. Kljuic: Unless compelled, you are saying you do refuse to bring this material with you. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I could be compelled to provide them. This is my private property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, that is another issue altogether. I think we have it. I'll take it, Mr. Kljuic, that you are saying no, unless somebody compels me -- another question altogether -- I will not bring this stuff to The Hague. I'm going to take it that's your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first interfere for one second, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Kljuic, you said I'm not willing, and your explanation mainly is you would rather first publish what you're preparing. And do I understand you well that you say Well, if I bring this material, my position as an author would be endangered because everyone could use it. Is that your fear? Because we then could try to see whether any solution could be found for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what, I lived in the communist regime where people could come to your house and seize your property. I don't think that that would happen today. But a second point is that this isn't the kind of document that the Prosecution has with dates, et cetera, et cetera. I have been a journalist for many years. These are a part of my observations, my personal records, things I noted down. So it is only I who can find my way in those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljuic, the issue is, first of all, that diaries or notebooks have assisted this Chamber in understanding the events at those times. We see many witnesses who are willing to make their notes or their diaries available. And of course, whether what the use of it is something that can be considered at a later stage, perhaps without your help we could not understand most of it; that's possible. And when you say that these notes are not available to the Prosecution, it almost goes without saying that if you would bring them or if you would provide copies in advance, then of course the Prosecution would have them as well. The parties are in that respect equal, and if it's relevant material it should be disclosed to the other party especially when questions will be put to you in respect of those notes. I do understand your fears in respect of other people using it when you're still preparing your publications. On the other hand, these notes, of course I have no idea yet how important they could be, but could assist us in finding the truth. It's for certain that what's written down at the time sometimes reflects in more detail or reflects with more position what at those times was observed by the author of the notes. Sometimes it helps to -- well, to remember things that would not be easily remembered without this, as the French say it, aide memoire. So therefore, it is for Mr. Stewart and for this Court, and I take it it's the same for the Prosecution, it's just a matter of not ignoring material that could eventually assist us in finding the truth. That's the issue. Therefore, I'd like you to perhaps consider this issue and, again, perhaps after the next break that we would get a final answer of you on whether you would be willing to bring them to The Hague on a voluntary basis or to provide copies. But I just explained this in a bit more detail to you because that's what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The English said aide memoire as well. We like to mine the richness of the French language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to respond to what I just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, these are my private notes. They have no official status whatsoever. If you want me to, I could recount a detail that I took note of from the one-on-one meeting I had with Mr. Karadzic. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no. At this moment, I'm not asking you for further details of your meeting with Karadzic because that's -- these are questions to be put to you by Mr. Stewart. But I was just addressing you in general terms. Even if these notes as usual have no official status and even if they are private notes -- of course, if there were private matters in it sometimes that you would say, well, this is not something to be made public, then of course it could always be considered. But just the question is whether by providing these notes, perhaps under conditions further to be considered, whether you would be willing to give them voluntarily or not. But think it over. I'm not urging you to answer it immediately. But what I wanted to make clear to you, that it's not intrusion in your private life; it's not to give them any official status, but not to ignore material that could possibly be of assistance in finding the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for that. And I also, although there are lots and lots of comments that spring to mind, I won't make them at the moment. May I simply make this observation, Your Honour, when Your Honour refers contingently to conditions, it may be - and Your Honour has only said that at this point - that none of us really says anything more about that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Conditions, of course, could never go against, I would say, fundamental procedural issues. That's, of course, clear. But if I would have -- if I would write a diary and if I would have some quite irrelevant personal matters in it, then, of course, I could say if this and this is not going to be made public, then I'm willing to give it to you. Otherwise, I have some reservations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's standard practice in all jurisdictions that entirely personal stuff unrelated to the case is held back from anybody that has no right to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I won't go any more into that because it's a bit abstract, then, unless and until we see some of this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it also though follows as a practical matter that I would reserve exploration of some of the content of these meetings and discussions pending consideration of this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Kljuic, let's go back to what we were talking about. At the moment I'm primarily interested in establishing the frequency and the nature of the meetings you had, rather than getting into the depth of discussions at this point. Dr. Karadzic, we're talking about. We were talking about up to April 1991. I'd like now, please, to take - it's convenient to take the next six-month period. Let's take from April to October. I think that would be April to October 1991. During that period, again, being as specific as you can, Mr. Kljuic, to help the Trial Chamber, what was the nature and the frequency of your meetings, contacts with Dr. Karadzic during that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, we see the start of the aggression against Croatia. The situation became complicated. The meetings no longer had the warmth that they had previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, start with the question, and then we'll see whether there's a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think Mr. Kljuic was answering the question. The question was what was the nature, frequency of the visits. There are two questions in that, and Mr. Kljuic is entitled to respond to the nature of the visits and put into context the visits because he was specifically asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it isn't really. When the witness talks about the start of the aggression against Croatia, it's just not necessary. I'm trying to help, Your Honour, to speed it along

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you would perhaps say this is the first part of my question and this is the second part of my question. If you do that, I certainly think that you'll get the answers you want. It's not incomprehensible how the witness responded to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not incomprehensible. It just wasn't an answer. I'll do what Your Honour says, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, how many times do you -- leaving aside those incidental, social type of contacts that you referred to, that category of meetings at the theatre, literary societies, put those totally on one side. Leaving those aside, how many times do you say you were in contact with Dr. Karadzic during that six-month period, April 1991 to October 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, not as frequently as before. And the talks had an exclusively political character. They were political dialogues because of the events in Croatia, because of what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you talk about --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the talks," then, you are referring to something which can sensibly be described as a meeting where you and both Dr. Karadzic were present at which, for example, you both sat down? Is that a fair description?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. For instance, there were meetings in parliament, meetings of parliament, of the government, of the leadership of the assembly, meetings between the three parties. And I'd like to tell you, Mr. Stewart, also, that I am a man that speaks very clearly. I'm a professor. I'm a journalist. And I'm very surprised that you're interrupting me when I'm trying to tell you what the nature of my meetings was during the second six months. During the first six months, neither Radovan Karadzic nor the SDS nor Milosevic, indeed, during that period of time had set out their projects. They had not implemented it either. It was only when the conflicts happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me again stop you. Mr. Stewart would like to know how often in that period of time you met Mr. Karadzic. Whether you are surprised that Mr. Stewart interrupted you where, as I see it, you more or less depicted the atmosphere rather than the type of meeting -- you were talking about not the same warmth -- is not something we should further discuss at this moment. But Mr. Stewart would like to know how often in this second six-month period you met with Dr. Karadzic in a meeting where you really talked to each other, which is usually done when you sit down but not necessarily. Could you tell us: During this six months, was that 20 times a month? Was it 10 times a month? What was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first six months, as I said, we met about three times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you about the second six months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And I had four or five intimate conversations with him, just the two of us, tete-a-tete. Now, during the second six months, we certainly met once in ten days. And during those six months, we had two conversations alone without any third party attending, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those are clear answers to the questions. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, during that six-month period, two meetings at which just you and Dr. Karadzic were present. Were there other sit-down meetings at which you and Dr. Karadzic and other people were present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And leaving aside assembly meetings, how many such meetings do you say there were during that six-month period? By such meetings, the meetings at which you and Dr. Karadzic were present but not just the two of you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps four or five, and they were meetings of the leaders of all the political parties who had their representatives in parliament. And they discussed the relationship towards the Yugoslav People's Army, the constitutional setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the same way, I don't want to explore the broader issues, but just specifically on the question of whether you did or you didn't, did you take notes of all those meetings during that period? That's to say, the tete-a-tetes between you and Dr. Karadzic and those other meetings at which there were some other people present.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take notes, but I did write down the basic positions assumed not only by Dr. Karadzic but the representatives of other political parties as well. That was my duty, for me to be able to report on this at the meetings of the HDZ leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you didn't take notes, there wasn't any change in your practice between the first six-month period that we asked about up to April 1991 and the next six months so far as note-taking was concerned, was there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just noted down the thesis, the most important details which were characteristic. As to the atmosphere and general mood that prevailed and all the rest, I'm not a shorthand typist. I don't take down everything word for word, just the basic premises. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to explore for the moment certainly the extent or nature of the notes in any detail, Mr. Kljuic. But you took some such notes of those other meetings at which there were other people present in addition to you and Dr. Karadzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it would be convenient perhaps to take the next six-month period, then. We'll keep it in chunks of six months. So from October 1991 through to April 1992, first of all, how many, if any, tete-a-tete meetings do you say you had with Dr. Karadzic during that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One. Just one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you date that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact date. I don't remember. But it took place in the premises of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put a rough date on it? It is a six-month period. Can you put it somewhere within that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of November, the beginning of December. At the insistence of Dr. Karadzic through one of my representatives whose name was Pasko Vukoje. And if need be, he can come and testify and say that the meeting did indeed come about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I didn't ask you that. So please, again, just answer the questions. Mr. Kljuic, how much of that other category of meeting, that's to say where you and Dr. Karadzic and at least one or more other persons were present, did you have during that six-month period, from October 1991 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "several" is a fairly elastic term, Mr. Kljuic. Can you be more specific about what "several" is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Between 10 and 15, let's say, during those six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your note-taking practice remain consistently the same as it had been during those previous two periods of six months each?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the meetings resembled each other. Karadzic would set the same ultimatums on different occasions, so they were more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Kljuic, is it this, that your practice didn't change, but actually there were simply less need to write stuff down because Mr. Karadzic was repeating the same position?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The during that -- those same periods, and I would like to try and take this next bit as quick and succinctly as we can, Mr. Kljuic, that applies to everything, but particularly here. I want to ask you particularly about Mrs. Plavsic. Let's take the same six-month periods, so from October 1990 to April 1991, did you have any tete-a-tete meetings with Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have, when she was in the company of her brother. We had been friends for many years. It wasn't a political meeting, it was a private meeting. And I would sit next to Mrs. Plavsic in the Presidency, so we would see each other every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kljuic. I'll try and short-circuit this, then. If we leave aside any meetings at which there was -- if such meetings took place, no political discussion at all, if that's realistic, over the whole period, from November 1990 through to April 1992, did you have any tete-a-tete meetings with Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Koljevic, again, if we leave aside, if it's realistically possible, any meetings at which you and he might not discuss anything political at all. Did you have any tete-a-tete meetings with Mr. Koljevic during the whole of that period, November 1990 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because professor Koljevic was the president of the board for foreign policy of the Presidency, just as Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kljuic. I apologise for interrupting you, except the answer "yes" to that question is enough. And then I can ask you further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's appropriate for the witness to give a brief explanation as to why he did have the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it isn't. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I beg your pardon for interrupting Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, if the witness thinks that something was really missing. But we have a different experience. So therefore, under the present circumstances, if there's anything which is beyond the question which you think is of such importance that we should know, you may address me. But first -- it could well that be the next question exactly asks you what you're saying. So first answer the questions of Mr. Stewart. And if at the end there would be something you say, well, this really gives a wrong impression of what happened, then you can address me, and you'll be allowed to add a few things. But try to stick to the questions to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I observe, of course I a hundred per cent agree with Your Honour's observation that any answer which would be misleading or wrong in some way without a qualification, the qualification is entirely legitimate. That's not an example. But may I say, Your Honour, if I do, as I'm trying to do, loyally follow Your Honour's suggestion that I should break the questions down specifically it's only fair then the witness doesn't himself decide which questions he's going to answer because that's my decision as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's clear. Mr. Harmon, we all are aware that getting the answers close to what the questions were is not the easiest thing over these last couple of days. And on the one hand, as the parties know, I usually allow some elaborations on issues close to the question, and the parties are wise enough not to object against such answers to be given. But I think we are a bit in a special situation. It's like a referee in the beginning of a football match, Mr. Harmon. You know what his task is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Your Honour. The question was did you have these kind of meetings with Mr. Koljevic. And the witness answered yes, he did, because he was the president of the board, of the foreign policy board. I think that's a perfectly appropriate expansion on the answer "yes." And therefore, I would ask, Your Honour, having been in the courtroom these past three days, I understand the position Your Honour is referring to, but I don't want to have the witness to be put in such a straightjacket that he feels he can only give a brief and uninformative answer. I think it is important when we touch upon the nature of this that we don't limit Mr. Kljuic to giving reasonable and brief expansions on the questions that are asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let's try not to spend all of our time on this procedural debate. As you may have noticed, the Chamber supports your approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand, if it becomes too rigid, finally, it might not serve its purpose any more. So if the one line would be added, then it takes less time to let that happen than to start procedural debates on that. So you would keep in mind that strictness sometimes allows for some flexibility. And then at the same time I'm asking the witness to very carefully listen to the questions put to you and first start answering them. Sometimes you might elaborate on issues which this Chamber has heard already five or ten times, for example, what positions people held, et cetera, is well known to this Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'm now trying to remember exactly where we were. We had established that you did have meetings with Mr. Koljevic, that you did have tete-a-tete meetings with Mr. Koljevic. I think I was asking you about the first six-month period, but that's what I'm going to do anyway. November 1990 to April 1991, how many tete-a-tete meetings, if any, during that period did you have with Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, yes, we did meet. You needn't doubt that. Second, we were members of the Presidency. We had our offices next to one another. And thirdly, Mr. Koljevic was the president of the foreign policy board of the Presidency of which I was a member. So we compiled a proposal for the foreign policy strategies of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I can say that I met him several times, a number of times, in the Presidency and less as an SDS official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, how many times?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have now explained to us. I instruct you: If you're asked how many times, first to tell us how many times. Because you used now five or six or seven lines, and we still do not know the answer to the question. How often did you have these tete-a-tete meetings with Dr. Koljevic during the first six-month period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four to five official meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You put in a qualification "official meetings." And I invited you to discard entirely social meetings. When you say official meetings, can we be clear, leaving aside any incidental social meetings at which there was no political discussion at all, the number of meetings you describe as being official meetings, that is the number of meetings, overall, tete-a-tete that you had with Mr. Koljevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that six-month period, November 1990 to April 1991, how many -- the same type of meeting did you have but at which there was somebody other than you and Professor Koljevic present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several meetings, because the three of us were members of the delegation in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they had meetings with all the other leaderships from the other republics in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you were invited first to say approximately several. Could be 2, could be 10, could be 20. How many? Approximately; if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not a statistics expert. We had five official meetings with five other republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us in numbers how many, approximately. If you can't, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had five meetings for sure because Bosnia and Herzegovina held five official meetings with five other republics. Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Koljevic, and myself were part of the delegation. That means that we travelled together. We stayed in Belgrade, in Zagreb, in Titograd, and the Slovenians and Macedonians came to see us so we held discussion, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from those meetings you just mentioned, those five, were there any others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were various meetings of an operational kind. As members of the Presidency, we were constantly together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't say. That was so frequent. That was a six-month period, and we would go to work every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, frequent means every day? Approximately, on the average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps not every day but very frequently because as members of the Presidency, we would receive various ambassadors, EU delegations, NATO delegations, American mediators. This was a very intense political life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three times a week? Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, what I'm trying to do -- just so that you know, it might be helpful as a background to the question. I'm trying, so far as possible, to put on one side contacts which were not really meetings. So let me just give you an example which I hope will help. If you and Professor Koljevic are there on the same occasion when there's some visiting dignitary or visiting politician or somebody important in town and you're there on the same occasion, whether it's a lunch or a drink or something like that, but your contact with Professor Koljevic is incidental, you may be introduced at the same time, you may have just a brief conversation in passing or something, I'm not asking you about those because, may I say, Mr. Kljuic, I understand that where you worked and the nature of your work, there might be lots and lots and lots of those. I'm wanting particularly to ask you about two categories of meeting. One is when I'm asking about is a particular person, tete-a-tete meetings with that person; and the other category is meetings with that person at which there were -- there's at least one other person present, so it wasn't tete-a-tete, but which was a meeting at which there was discussion, and you and that person were participants in the discussion. Is that a clear -- is that a clear description, a clear categorisation for you, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we call those, please, categories A and B, if you like. A is tete-a-tete, and B is the other type. I want to get through this as quickly as possible, this background basic stuff. In relation to the next two six-month periods, so that's April 1991 through to October 1991, and then October 1991 through to April 1992, all I really want from you at this stage as best you can do is a number in category A and a number in category B. I just want to know in the six-month period, first of all, April 1991 to October 1991, how many meetings as best you can remember in category A, tete-a-tete?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, are we referring to meetings with Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Thank you for -- in case there was any misunderstanding, we are with Professor Koljevic at the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 10 and 15 meetings in category A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in category B, where there were other people present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of such meetings because we had sessions very frequently, two or three times a week. There was a lot of diplomatic action because in the Presidency we were all responsible for certain fields. You should be aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to give a number. It's obviously not likely to be an exact number, Mr. Kljuic. But please try to give a number in the way that you did for category A?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He did respond "two or three times a week." That is a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd invite Mr. Harmon to just let me pursue this because -- well, I won't say because. I'll put it a different way, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Kljuic, then, that over that six-month period, there were something between 50 and 70 meetings --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, QED.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, then, you're not saying that. So it's not two or three times a week arithmetically. During that six-month period, April 1991 to October 1991, we're talking about Professor Koljevic, category B, how many meetings do you say you had, Professor Koljevic, and at least Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond one other person was present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps between 20 and 30 such meetings. I must say that I don't understand why you are insisting on this number because these are statistics. If you want to know what the relation was like, you can obtain this information in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it's up to Mr. Stewart whether he would like to know the numbers. And we'll find out during his next questions or in relation to other questions how he wants to establish the kind of relationship you had. But the frequency also in numbers of meetings is not necessarily irrelevant in that respect. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Kljuic, then, following up to the next six-month period from October 1991 through to April 1992, Professor Koljevic. How many meetings in category A, tete-a-tete?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps one during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many meetings during that period in category B? That's to say you, Professor Koljevic, and at least one other person present at a meeting.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10 and 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Mr. Krajisnik. We'll go through the same sequence. November 1991 -- I'm sorry. November 1990, correction. November 1990 through to April 1991, did you have any tete-a-tete meetings with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So category A is a nil return. Zero in category A. Category B, meetings at which you, Mr. Krajisnik, and at least one other person were present. How many of those do you say there were in the six-month period November 1990 to April 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of such meetings since Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the assembly, and the Presidency always proposed an agenda, or rather, they proposed items that the Presidency wanted to see discussed at the assembly. And during that time, I attended meetings with Mr. Krajisnik when the leaders of the HDZ, the SDS, and the SDA were present and the HDZ and SDS had bilateral meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you give that -- a number as well. Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said between 10 and 20 such meetings during that six-month period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's, then, not on the record. You said there were a number of such meetings. But I do understand that you count them at anything between 10 and 20. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next six-month period then. We have got this echo back. Never mind. In the next six-month period, April 1991 through to October 1991, do you say that you had any tete-a-tete meetings, that's category A, with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as the category B meetings are concerned, you, Mr. Krajisnik, and at least one other person at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 20 meetings or perhaps more. I'm including the parliament and the Presidency meetings, governmental meetings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say -- I know it's difficult to draw perhaps absolutely clear distinctions, Mr. Kljuic. I'd acknowledge that. But I was rather inviting to you exclude the parliament. So if you take out Assembly sessions, what's your answer, category B, period April 1991 to October 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't exclude the assembly period, the assembly, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, with respect, I can exclude them because I can and have excluded them from my question. So you would focus on my question, from which the assembly sessions are excluded. Please answer; the number of meetings in category 2 from your recollection during that period April 1991 to October 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I was interested in Mr. Krajisnik as the president of the assembly and as one of the main leaders of the SDS. Whenever we had contact, this was the subject that was discussed. If you are interested in this fact, we weren't very close to each other. I was a lot closer to Mrs. Plavsic, to Koljevic, and even to Karadzic. I was much closer to them than even to Mr. Krajisnik, if that's what you want to hear. But at that time, I was a member of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, again. What Mr. Stewart wants to know: How many of those approximately 20 you mentioned were assembly meetings? That means official assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let me go for one second. Mr. Kljuic, you said there were 20 meetings or perhaps more. How many would be approximately official assembly meetings, so the assembly convening as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can divide this. Half of them had to do with the assembly and were in the assembly, and half of the other political meetings were held outside of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, could I say that this echo which has come back is really quite terrible. Of course, I can carry on, but I don't know if anybody else has got it. But I would appreciate it if it could be worked on. I don't know whether other people have got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no echoes on ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I really do, Your Honour. And I've replugged into the next place here as well, and I get the same. It comes and goes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has happened to me in the past as well, and I think it has to be with a button that has been pushed or moved on the top. I'm not an expert, but I know it can be regulated fairly quickly. But I'm not an expert, and I don't know which particular button it is. It might be a knob on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Harmon's help. The day that Mr. Harmon and I give each other advice on technical matters, then everybody has a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is becoming any better?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I have to say something to see whether -- yes, Your Honour, it's better. Thank you very much, whoever -- thank you. Yes, that's much better. Thank you. Excuse me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So yes, by one route or another, we've got to the broad conclusion that during that six-month period, October 1991 to April 1992 -- excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I had just lost track of whether I had asked him about the last six-month period, October 1991 to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the last question was about April 1991 until October 1991. You find that on page 66 on line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour, that was my concern. I didn't want to go over the same ground again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as that six-month period from April to October 1991 is concerned, I think we've got to this position that the category B meetings, leaving aside assembly, so the meetings at which Mr. Krajisnik, you, and at least one other person were present, something like about 10 or something like that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So moving on to the next six-month period, October 1991 to April 1992. Do you say that you and Mr. Krajisnik had any tete-a-tete meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not outside of the institutions. But in the assembly, I would have personal contact with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kljuic, let's try and be as unambiguous about this as we can. What I had understood you to mean by a tete-a-tete meeting -- but to be clear what I am meaning by the question of a tete-a-tete meeting is a meeting where you and Mr. Krajisnik, just the two of you, had at least some serious discussion about some political, in the broader sense, some political matter. Is that a clear enough description of the category of the type of meeting? Do you understand that description sufficiently clearly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your description is clear to me, you know. But you don't understand how we lived and worked. Five minutes in the assembly in such a tense atmosphere when the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina is at stake can result in far more than a 12-hour long meeting at which coffee and mineral water is provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I don't want to debate with you that sort of understanding or misunderstanding. As a starting point, you confirmed very helpfully that my description of the kind of meeting I was going to ask you about was sufficiently clear for your purposes. So that type of tete-a-tete meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, did you have any of those during the period October 1991 to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That type of meeting, a meeting that was arranged through a secretary, a meeting at which we sat down, we didn't have such meetings, but we did have tete-a-tete meetings in institutions. But you must understand me. Krajisnik wasn't a partner of mine. Mr. Krajisnik's partner in the HDZ was Mariofil Ljubic who was at a lower rank. Karadzic and Izetbegovic were my partners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who exactly was Mariofil Ljubic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-president of the parliament. A Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so summarise, when you say that Mr. Krajisnik's partner in the HDZ was Mariofil Ljubic, you mean effectively that he was Mr. Krajisnik's opposite number?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the second by rank in the assembly. He wasn't his opposite number because Mr. Krajisnik had a far more important rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's -- I'm just trying to clarify that. And it's translation questions here as well. But when you say "partner," they're in different parties -- Let me try it another way, Mr. Kljuic. You seem to have been saying that when you had a meeting, then the appropriate person for you to meet would have been Dr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to cut this short. Did you intend to say that if you would meet representatives of the other party, that you would meet with the party leaders, Izetbegovic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem I have at the moment is I distinctly remember the witness -- yes, exactly. Where is it? I distinctly remember the witness referring to Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic, and I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness now confirmed that, and I put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is solved now because it has got dropped from the transcript in the moment. No doubt it will be put back in that. That was my confusion. I had a clear recollection of that, Your Honour, but couldn't see it on the screen. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you were saying in summary, yes, just supplementing His Honour's question then. The appropriate persons for you to meet were Izetbegovic and Karadzic; the appropriate person for your colleague, I think Mr. Ljubic, your colleague, to meet was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's at stake were the problems we were dealing with in the parliament. Mr. Krajisnik as a Serb was the president, and the Croat Mario Ljubic, was the vice-president. They worked on problems that had to do with parliamentary procedure, on the contents of the parliament's work, and on the function of the parliament in order to create a new society. As far as meetings at which decisions could be obtained are concerned or at which agreements could be reached, then this concerned Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Karadzic and myself. However, there were a lot of combined meetings which were attended by two or three or five people from each party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just be clear, then, Mr. Kljuic. Category B, we're talking about meetings at which you and -- we're now talking about Mr. Krajisnik. You, Mr. Krajisnik, and other persons or at least one other person were present. During that six-month period, October 1991 to April 1992, how many such meetings do you say that there were? And I'm excluding, please, assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were over ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just over ten, just to be clear. Do you say of the order of 10 or 12? Something like that? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten to twelve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're quite close to 12.30, if that weren't an inconvenient point for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, we'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, of course, the Chamber has given it some thought on what happens. And if it would assist you that sometimes rather than going back right to the beginning and going through the same problems again might not always be the most efficient solution, whereas picking up what is in the answer in order to further develop that. I refer you to the matter of 20 inclusive or exclusive. If you take up the answer and try to find what you want instead of going back saying that the question has been misunderstood, that might -- it's just a suggestion, because we're all facing the same problem. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll do my best, as usual, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, then you say in your evidence, and this -- you have said in your evidence in this case, and that was at page 18, for the record of Monday's transcript, 27th September, you said you met Mr. Krajisnik in 1990 during the election campaign. "Later, when he was president of the parliament we had a series of contacts, all the more so because as a member of the Presidency, I attended every parliament session. And in addition to that, in all major negotiations between the party, the SDS was mostly represented by Karadzic and Krajisnik whereas I at the time was a leading representative of the HDZ. Apart from that, I spoke to Mr. Krajisnik several times in the course of official talks between the HDZ and the SDS." And Mr. Kljuic, we can confirm, can we, it logically follows, but I want to be clear so there's no misunderstanding, when you say you spoke to Mr. Krajisnik several times in the course of official talks, that was always in the company of at least one other person, and in practice several people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about official talks between the HDZ and the SDS, not all of the category B meetings that you have described, those are not the tete-a-tete meetings but the ones where there were other people present, not all of those are what you would describe as official talks between the HDZ and the SDS, are they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those official meetings, there were breaks, or rather pauses. Sometimes people would speak at once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic -- [Previous interpretation continues] ... what's happening now. Mr. Kljuic, could you answer my question, please. Do you agree that not all of the category B meetings, that's the ones where there were other people present but you and Mr. Krajisnik were there -- not all of those meetings were what you have described as official talks between the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond HDZ and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you were going on then to talk about breaks. I'm going to invite you. What were you going to explain about the breaks in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of open questions on certain issues, and individuals on both sides would sometimes address other individuals whom they felt could -- whom they felt they could achieve an agreement with and that this would not detract from the overall negotiations. And this was particularly true of the first stage of the constitution of power and authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it sounds, tell me whether this is wrong it. It sounds as if what you're describing as far as the meetings are concerned is really a normal dynamic of a meeting, that if you have a number of people around the room, of course depending on their particular positions, it may be that anybody at the meeting might address anybody else at the meeting. Do you confirm what you're talking about is actually relatively normal dynamics of a group meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes, but no, not everybody could address anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to go further into that, Your Honour. You talked about Mr. Milosevic in your evidence. You said it was evident that Slobodan Milosevic, and this is page 18 of Monday's transcript, was the vehicle implementing a project that had been developed by the intellectual circles in the Serbian Academy of Sciences. Now, are you talking about a project that has commonly gone under the label of "Greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, that project of a Greater Serbia and the memorandum had a practical aspect which was known under the code name of RAM, R-A-M.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you drawing a distinction between -- this is a memorandum produced by a group of intellectuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the traditions of Serbian policies and politics of the 19th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're saying, are you -- are you saying there was distinction between the content of that memorandum and the RAM plan, or that the RAM plan was simply a development of that memorandum?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference, no distinction. However, the memorandum and the idea of a Greater Serbia, they did not designate how this was to be implemented. But the RAM plan understood the implementation of that project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you -- well, when did you first hear of the RAM plan?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first heard about it in the summer of 1991, having heard a secret conversation between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic, and I went public with that information at a conference of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to hear a secret conversation between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thanks to certain police services, the Minister of the Interior told me of this tape, of the recording. I just listened to it. I wasn't able to have it in my possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do? You went to the police station, did you, and this person played it to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The Minister brought it to me to my office, to my cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what was the RAM plan? Was the content of the RAM plan discussed in that conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Milosevic, not Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I said Mr. Krajisnik, I apologise then. It has been corrected. So was the content of the RAM plan discussed in that conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Karadzic modified the concept of RAM, which had a completely different meaning, into a Muslim name, RAM or RAMO. And that was supposed to detract anybody listening in from what it actually was. But quite obviously, they were dealing with the implementation of the Greater Serbia project where it is precisely stated that they should go to General Uzelac in Banja Luka, that they would get weapons, that he had already secured certain areas and so on. And many other things. So that was the first time that we actually learned of the existence of a project like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what were -- did you learn the essential features of the RAM plan from that conversation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course -- and I've said this a number of times, that the Bosnian Serbs were in charge of a part of the general project which was led by Milosevic, so for the realisation of something that was to have been put into practice on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina along with subordination and using the forces of the Croatian Serbs in Knin and Eastern Slavonia. Since Banja Luka was, in a certain sense, the centre of the region, and General Uselac was the commander with broad competencies and authority and even greater materiel potential, Karadzic and Milosevic were discussing how Uselac would go about putting his task into practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek clarification. Was this an intercept of a telephone conversation or of a -- let's say, live meeting, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened to the tape, a recording of a telephone conversation between Karadzic and Milosevic. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those features which you described in your last answer before that one, those were matters that you learned, did you, from listening to the tape of that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although we knew before that there was a project in existence. But this was very concrete and specific. Certain facts were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you say were the -- at the time when you heard this, what were the essential features of the plan?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the essential features were these: In Croatia, for example, there was already a conflict along those lines. The external western borders, for example, of the territory that Milosevic wished to unite. So the Serbs of Croatia held those positions already, which were to represent the western borders of a Serbian state, but the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina remained unsolved. What had to be now done was to undertake preparations and arming so that when the time was ripe, the territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina could be taken over which would be kept within that new state as provided for by the RAM plan or operation. So that is 70 per cent or 75 per cent, roughly speaking, of today's Bosnia-Herzegovina. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about your political contacts with Mr. Milosevic. Again, page 18 of Monday's transcript, 27th September. You said -- well, I'll ask you about the same -- well, first of all, have you ever had any tete-a-tete meeting with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you're asking me to say, I have never been with Milosevic. But I faced him eye to eye during a luncheon in Belgrade where he took me to one side and explained to me that he supported the departure of Western Herzegovina which was populated almost exclusively by Croats, that it should move to a Croatian state. In this entire process, they tried to separate Western Herzegovina out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, away from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that idea was very much present in the minds of certain Croats; that is to say, that these should finally join up with the Croatian state. However, this would mean breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state; and secondly, I was not an advocate of this type of political view. I was a Bosnian-Herzegovinian integralist, and I said to Milosevic on that particular occasion that we don't understand each other when we -- when it comes to what Western Herzegovina actually is. And then he said quite clearly that it was the right bank of the River Neretva, and that the left bank belonged to the Serbs which was the same thing that Momo Mandic had said to Bruno Stojic and Branko Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this luncheon, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, he was in Belgrade. But I met Milosevic briefly once in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So when you say in the autumn of 1991 he was in Belgrade, you're saying that was the occasion of that luncheon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you met him briefly once in Sarajevo. What were the circumstances -- first of all, when was that occasion in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in autumn 1991. The leadership of all six republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a series of meetings and sessions in all the capital cities of the republics. And one of those meetings was organised in Sarajevo at Stojcevac, and that's when I had a meeting with Mr. Tudjman as well. But in the meantime, since the two of them had contacts, I joined in and, of course, Milosevic welcomed me, said hello. He encouraged me and so on. But I didn't meddle and interfere in the conversation. What I did was I listened to what Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic were saying. That was another break in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Sarajevo occasion before or after the Belgrade lunch that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event in Sarajevo came afterwards, but they're well-known dates and you can check them up and establish them very easily. There are documents to bear them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, not all lunches are documented, Mr. Kljuic. The occasion of the luncheon, that's documented under what label or description of the event?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had an official meeting of the delegations of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina first, and Mr. Milosevic was in the Serbian delegation. The president of the assembly was Trifunovic, and the prime minister was Unkovic. And in the Bosnian BH delegation, there were three members of the Presidency. Izetbegovic chaired the meeting, Mr. Koljevic and myself. It was a working day the entire day. We just took a break for lunch, and it might have lasted for, say, two hours. And it was during that luncheon that I was placed to Mr. Milosevic so that we talked throughout lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- have you ever had telephone conversations with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was present when Mr. Izetbegovic and Milosevic were engaged in a conversation. And on that occasion, Mr. Izetbegovic said "Mr. Kljuic is here with us; he's listening in."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were listening in to both sides of the conversation, were you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. You could do that on the telephone apparatus. You could put the volume up and hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the topic or content of that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because of the war in Croatia at the time, we had a change in the attitude taken by the population towards the JNA. Parents were hiding their children. They were sending them off abroad. They were smuggling them out of the country. In simple terms, the citizens did not want their children to go to the war in Croatia as part of the JNA. And I have to say that that was not characteristic only of the Croats and Muslims, but a large number of Serbs didn't allow their children to join up and go to the army. So during this period of time through the media and in other ways, attempts were made to lend support to the Yugoslav People's Army. And Milosevic at that point in time told Mr. Izetbegovic, he said to him, "You know that the Yugoslav People's Army is the sole, official army belonging to all our nations and nationalities or ethnicities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from the conversation which you had with Mr. Milosevic at that lunch in Belgrade, how many times in your lives do you say that you have had a conversation with Mr. Milosevic which touched upon the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I had occasion to say hello to Mr. Milosevic on several occasions, but the only detailed conversation and discussion about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the meeting we had in Belgrade, or rather the encounter when in a pause during lunch, he took me to one side and said -- or rather, and told me what I've already told you, that he wanted Western Herzegovina to be joined to Croatia, et cetera. And later on, he dictated all the places which he considered belonged to the Croats in that division of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when earlier this week at page 18, for other people's record, of Monday, 27th September transcript, when you said, referring to Mr. Milosevic, "the subject of our conversations concentrated on efforts to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina," in fact we're talking about a single conversation, that one in Belgrade at that lunch.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't discuss that at other places, and I wasn't the opposite number of Mr. Milosevic, whereas Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Kiro Gligorov were. They were on a par at the same level. But let me explain, during that luncheon, it wasn't a discussion at lunch, during lunch. We went to a separate part of the hall because it was a large hall and discussed this matter for 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kljuic. And you said in your evidence, same page reference in the transcript, following your reference to that, you said, "however, to his great regret," and that's Mr. Milosevic, "I," Mr. Kljuic, "was not a good partner for that kind of agreement." That's relating to, obviously, from what you said to Western Herzegovina. From what you've said, Mr. Kljuic, it sounds as if -- would you agree, you weren't the person with whom Mr. Milosevic could and would have thought to reach such an agreement because you were not his opposite number?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, too. But I promoted the political programme of the Bosnian Croats, which was totally in opposition to the idea of a division. I was legally elected, not only at the elections where I received the relative majority of votes, although the Croatian ticket was the smallest, but at the party convention on the 23rd and 24th of March 1991, I was given plebiscitory support of 258 delegates, deputies of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of a plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, then you said that -- this is page 19 of that same transcript - "as for the policy of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic relative to Bosnia and Herzegovina, he did not hide his plans; on the contrary." You said, "He tried to find in me a partner for that sort of thing." And can we take it that "that sort of thing," by that you meant the incorporation of Western Herzegovina in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you saw earlier, there were three options which the Serbs from Belgrade were interested in. And they were, first of all, a Greater Serbia; then secondly, the complete Bosnia-Herzegovina within the composition of the so-called Yugoslavia minus Croatia and Slovenia; and thirdly, what actually happened. That is to say, a war, and then a free-for-all to take as much as we can. I was not at all in favour of such a division, and I was especially not in favour of having all Croatian interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina being boiled down and reduced to the area in Western Herzegovina, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] just a moment, please, Mr. Stewart. [Interpretation] -- which was inhabited by barely 17 per cent of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So all those who accepted western Herzegovina to be the sole thing that the Croats had, they would be forfeiting 73 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to focus the questions so that when we have a phrase like "that sort of thing" we try to be ask specific as we can about what that means. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond You listed the three options. Now, clearly, you would agree the third of those options, I think as you put it, which was that there would be a war and a free-for-all, if option is the apt label. Nobody was seeking to find in you a partner for war, were they? You would agree that's absurd?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just moving away from the whole range of options. Let's be clear, please, Mr. Kljuic, when you say Mr. Milosevic was trying to find in you a partner for "that sort of thing," did that primarily mean the carving off of Western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, that would have satisfied the loudest portion of Croats from Western Herzegovina; secondly, cutting off just one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have disrupted the entire construction of the state itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And then what you said, Mr. Kljuic, in your evidence, and this is again specifically at page 19 of Monday, 27th September transcript, the complete sentence was "he tried" - Mr. Milosevic that was - "he tried to find in me a partner for that sort of thing, as did Karadzic." When did Dr. Karadzic first make an attempt to find in you, Mr. Kljuic, a partner for "that sort of thing," as you've described it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the aggression against Croatia, and that was May, the month of May 1991, Karadzic said that he was sorry that the conflict had come about, but that the separation -- that separation and delineation was the sole outcome that the Serbs wanted. He also said to me, "You take what is yours, and we'll take ours. And if there's something left over for the Muslims, a small portion of the territory, perhaps they'll be satisfied with what they get."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific occasion on which Dr. Karadzic first made that suggestion to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic never hid his views. He presented them many times. But if you want me to quote one such specific occasion, and a conversation that we had at the headquarters of the SDS, for example, then it went as follows --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, just for a moment, please. What I particularly asked you about, if you are able to answer this, what I was particularly asking you about what to identify, if you can, the first occasion on which Dr. Karadzic ever made that suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First occasion was in May of 1991, and then the occasion was repeated five times over the next month or two as the front in Croatia developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the nature of that first occasion, by which I mean what sort of meeting was it and who was there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was between the two of us, tete-a-tete, nobody else was in the room. Karadzic said quite clearly that the Serbs would take all the areas which they considered to belong to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place at the headquarters of Karadzic's party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At whose instigation or invitation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A common friend of ours who was related to a businessman called Ostojic. You've got to make a distinction between the businessman called Ostojic and the minister called Ostojic. He was asked to arrange for a discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, excuse me, there's a simple distinction between the minister called Ostojic and the businessman called Ostojic, to give their first names. What was the name of the businessman called Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Branko. I'm not sure. But he was a very influential businessman. And he asked a Croatian deputy in the parliament, his name is Pasko Vukoje, and the two of them married either two sisters or two cousins, I'm not quite sure. But their wives were related. And the reason was that these people were fighting in Croatia. Let's not fight in Bosnia. You representatives of the Serbs and Croats try to reach an agreement. You're on good terms. Let's try and prevent shooting from breaking out. What I always insisted on was that the Serbian leadership in Bosnia should condemn the crimes committed by the JNA and by the Serbs in Croatia in Croatia itself. And this is something that they never did. On the other hand, Karadzic said publicly, this was a very loud and severe speech, he said that the Serbs would take everything that they considered to be their own. Since this was heard in other rooms, too, this deputy of mine in the parliament, when he heard this loud discussion, he left. He left me. At that point, I told Karadzic, "Take everything that you can, but Bosnia and Herzegovina will survive." And later, this discussion frequently resumed. Things would cool down, and you would start talking normal again and in a friendly way, et cetera. But Karadzic complained to Milosevic and said that I wasn't a good person to talk to. He also said that I had been bought by the Muslims, and they went to Zagreb with these accusations. And one day, President Tudjman said "Stjepan, the Bosnian Serbs complain and say that you don't want to talk to them. This is pointless." I said, "That's not true. But if it's necessary, we can start talking tomorrow." I promised President Tudjman that we would start talking to each other. Later on, it was found out that Tudjman and Milosevic had some sort of a red telephone line. When I arrived in Sarajevo in the morning, I phoned Karadzic and I said, "Should we see each other?" He said, "Yes, I know we should." And that's when that famous meeting in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was held. It was held in Mr. Krajisnik's office, and this meeting was attended on the Croatian side by --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Kljuic. Don't worry, we are going to coming on to that meeting. It probably won't be today, but the famous meeting you describe, can we come to it, largely, at a moment of my choosing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've got 10 minutes to go to the normal time, and we did leave over certain issues, some of which won't directly involve Mr. Kljuic as the witness but in relation to the question of documents that he may have in Sarajevo. I don't wish the witness to leave The Hague without us taking whatever advantage is appropriate of his presence to explore such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we could deal with that in approximately five minutes, if you would stop in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kljuic, you made it clear, this is -- your evidence is perfectly clear on this, you made it clear to Dr. Karadzic that you did not agree with his proposal. That's absolutely clear, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you had been the first man -- this is, again, page 19 of Monday, the 27th September transcript. You were the first man to public the national programme of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina and you said the most important thing in that programme was for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain a sovereign republic; that is, to have the same status of the other former republics of Yugoslavia, a stand that was to be confirmed by the Badinter Commission. Mr. Kljuic, I just want to see whether you clearly agree with this: When you talk about "the most important thing in that programme being for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain a sovereign republic," you were not talking about maintaining the status quo, were you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "status quo."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were not talking about maintaining the position precisely as it was.
