utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the phrase "the most important thing was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain a sovereign republic." I'll put it more clearly and directly, then. To remain a sovereign republic with the same status as the other former republics of Yugoslavia, in fact, involved the highly significant change that Bosnia and Herzegovina would become a separate, independent sovereign state and leave the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your terminology, it would remain a sovereign republic, but then that's because you -- is this right? You regarded it as being a sovereign republic even when it was within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the republics according to the constitution of 1974 were practically states. We didn't break up Yugoslavia. It's not important to know who did. But when Croatia and Slovenia left Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia could no longer survive with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why? The system of governing Yugoslavia was based on a Presidency with eight members, and there were representatives of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Vojvodina, Kosovo, Montenegro, and Macedonia. In the course of 1990 and at the beginning of 1991, Milosevic had already withdrawn autonomy of Vojvodina and Kosovo, two autonomous provinces. And those representatives, one of which was an Albanian, were replaced by those people. So he had four votes in the Presidency. He only needed one more vote in order, for example, to introduce a military dictatorship. Once Slovenia and Croatia left such a Yugoslavia, then there were six votes left in the Presidency, and Milosevic had four of them. As a result, he had absolute power. That is why we couldn't remain in such a Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Kljuic. Your Honour, I notice it is now 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Kljuic, before the break, we discussed before the break whether you would be willing to bring your notes. Have you given it some further consideration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having thought about it a little, Your Honours, I don't think that they would be of much value to you. These are my personal observations that I wrote down in notebooks. The pages are torn out, put aside, what is important is information that I related at HDZ meetings or at Presidency meetings. But what is of particular interest for my book, for example, my book with Karadzic when I told him that Bosnia-Herzegovina will survive in one way or another, this is something that you have already heard. There are two or three examples of that. These notes haven't been sorted out. They don't have the form of a diary, of organised documents. Many of them don't even a have date. In some cases, you only have the initials of the participants. So I don't see what the value of these documents would be for you. If it is really necessary, I will bring two or three examples here to show you what they look like. It was written down rapidly. They are personal notes of mine, and they don't really have any value as documents that would be of interest for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to give us an opportunity to see whether we share your view, not just by examples? It might be that the parties and this Trial Chamber have other views on what is most relevant or less relevant or not relevant at all. It could be just a name; it could be just an expression which sounds familiar to us. My question, therefore, again, is would you be willing to bring them all or even to copy them and to send them to the Trial Chamber so that we are able -- I mean, if there are of no help, don't be afraid that we'll have used them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any secrets, you know. Throughout my lifetime, I have fought for certain ideals. And I have stated this quite clearly. I will provide you with two or three examples. I will send them to see whether they are of interest to you. I'm not sure you will be able to read anything because I have been using a typewriter for years so my handwriting is not very clear. I will send you two or three examples through a representative in Sarajevo. He can come to see me in about 15 days. I will send them to you and you can evaluate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can please send them all. And I assure you if we can't read your handwriting, then of course it's of no use for us to continue to read. If the material is irrelevant or if the material cannot be understood, then of course we would go just further. So if it would be possible to hand over the full set of the notes you have, we'll then be at least in a position to see whether it's...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's a huge amount of paper. And I'm writing a book that consists of 14 chapters. The first one deals with the fall of the Berlin Wall. The last one dealings with the Hague Tribunal. And once I have dealt with one field the papers that I prepared are destroyed, the text remains. I can provide you with a number of typed-out chapters that have been prepared for the book so you can see what my positions were. But as far as the matters that concern, the people who are mentioned here at the Tribunal are concerned, these were short notes for a meeting, things that I wrote down so that I could talk to my people in the HDZ about this, or that so that I could address the Presidency and tell them whether it was true that there was a desire to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were things to enable us to adopt a position, et cetera, et cetera. I could provide you with a number of chapters that are already completed and ready to be published if you're interested in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you would provide us with your interpretation of the facts, which, of course we heard something about that. This Chamber and the parties are mainly interested in the direct sources. Would it be possible for you -- the number of pages that would cover 1991, 1992, how many would that be approximately? I'm again asking for numbers. Approximately. Would that be 200 pages, 300 pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be about 360 A4 pages for the book. Right now, I probably have about 70 or 80 pages that are prepared for printing, about a quarter of the book. Everything else has been handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about your notes of that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these papers -- I'll have to go through them, separate them, and whatever is recorded I will provide you with that. Not only for the period that you are interested, but also for other periods. I will photocopy them and I will provide you with them. As to how useful they will be to you, believe me, I don't know. I have difficulty in finding me way around these papers too. But if this is your wish, not the wish of the Prosecution or of the Defence, I will provide you with these papers. I must tell you, though, that as soon as I return to Sarajevo tomorrow, I will be leaving for Germany where I'll spend 15 days at the Book Fair in Cologne because one of my books on Bosnia-Herzegovina will be promoted at that fair. It doesn't have any political content, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber very much appreciates your willingness to bring your personal notes. I do understand that you need some time to prepare because, well, if I'm preparing something in writing, it sometimes is also not all well organised. But would you be willing to see persons to assist you in copying? If you prepare the personal notes, as you explained that to us, just the writing down of positions taken by certain parties, et cetera, et cetera, so those person notes, not the preparatory works for your book, but especially those personal notes that you made at that time, then we'll ask the Victims and Witness section because it is at this moment not appropriate for the parties to speak with you. We'll ask, then, the Victims and Witness section, to assist you in having it copied, and then it will be sent to The Hague prior to you being recalled, because as you are now aware of, the cross-examination has not yet been concluded. Although I also appreciate that the latter part, I think the understanding between the examining party you as a witness became better, so we very much appreciate if you would, with this assistance, copy your personal notes. You can limit it to 1991, 1992 for the time being. We'll then look at it, and the parties will assist the Chamber in looking at whether they're of any use at all or whether we just send them back. If, however, you would bring the originals when you come back, but already give copies to the representative of the Victims and Witness unit. Yes? Thank you very much for your cooperation, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Am I to understand, Your Honour, that these notes, then, that Mr. Kljuic produces to the Chamber are not to be disseminated to anyone else outside of the parties themselves? That might give Mr. Kljuic some reassurance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I think the first thing we will do is to inspect them to see whether they are relevant or of any use to us in these proceedings. And of course it might be that at some later stage then in due course, maybe some elements will be dealt with in open session, but even then we could consider to deal with them in closed session. So if you send them to the Tribunal, I take it you agree with that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As a matter of physical sending, they get sent to the Tribunal, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kljuic, the parties will be instructed that if they assist the Chamber in seeing whether it's relevant or not, it's not something to be made public. We'll first look at it, and if some parts support your evidence or perhaps at a later stage during cross-examination reference might be made to that, even if the material is such that you wish it be dealt with in closed session, we'll consider that. So if you send it to us, it will not be public material right away. It would be confidential, at least for the whole bunch, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, could I observe that, yes, indeed, I had assumed and do confirm that of course we would expect to keep such material confidential. After all, we're only asking to see it in order to see whether it might form the subject of cross-examination. And then the question -- well, then, normally, it would simply be in open court, then. Your Honour, there is one, possibly two, further short observations, but they are more appropriately made after the witness has left Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Kljuic, you'll receive an invitation to appear again in this Tribunal in order to be further cross-examined. And perhaps the Judges have questions for you as well at the very end. Could you tell us anything about your availability in time. Are there certain periods? Well, perhaps, if you inform the Victims and Witness section, those who are accompanying you during your stay here in The Hague, if there are certain periods where you're certainly not available, that at least the Tribunal and then also the Office of the Prosecutor will know when you're not available. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, of course it occurs to me there is one matter which I ought to specifically raise before the witness leaves, and this is this: I wonder if through the Trial Chamber may I ask whether Mr. Kljuic would either be willing or be directed to deal with the matter in this way, that any questions transmitted to him while he is away from The Hague in this interim period as to what material he actually has gone, that he should answer those. Because Your Honour will see the difficulty if we're not able to in the interim while he's away from The Hague to explore that issue, the whole thing could be a complete mess when he comes back to The Hague. So can we be clear that any questions directed to Mr. Kljuic, which would go in writing, of course, as to what material he has, he would give that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, would it be a good idea that if there's any written communication with Mr. Kljuic when he's away concerning this material - I limit it to that - that it can be sent to him in writing with a copy to the Trial Chamber so that the Trial Chamber, and perhaps before sending the letter first send a copy of the letter intended to be sent to Mr. Kljuic to the Trial Chamber with a pause of one or two days so the Chamber at least keeps some control over the communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it should be sent in advance to the Trial Chamber and to us, if we have an issue on it, we can raise it with the Chamber before --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly had that in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kljuic, you have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would just like to say, don't be mistaken about these documents of mine. These are private documents, very brief. I think that you might consider them to be a very good source of information. But these are some of my thoughts about what was happening and perhaps some thoughts about private conversations. Secondly, if you send me questions in order to save time, I will provide you with written responses to those questions. And thirdly, it's only around mid-November that I could come to The Hague for a few days. I can't come next month, but in mid-November it would be possible for me to come here and spend another two or three days or how long is necessary in order to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, usually the parties are not allowed to contact you once your examination has started. The Chamber now allow the parties, if they have specific questions to you in relation to the material you're going to send to the Tribunal, that first the Chamber gets a copy of the letter they intend to send to you. And would you please, if you respond to those letters, send a copy to the Trial Chamber so that the Chamber is aware of what kind of contacts are there, since you have not concluded your cross-examination. I very much thank you for coming to The Hague, at least this first time. I thank you for your cooperation as far as the notes are concerned. And we'll see you back then most likely somewhere in November. Thank you. Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there's one other issue, I believe. And I am aware that I forgot to thank the interpreters the last time, that I'm too often -- I should have stopped at five minutes past, half past two instead of saying that we had another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Our thanks as well, Your Honour. It's only this, that we do agree that if Mr. Kljuic is actually sending material, that it should be sent, when I say to the Tribunal, I presume to the Trial Chamber would be appropriate as the forwarding. But we take it that when that material arrives, then the -- of course the Prosecution and Defence, both of us, the Trial Chamber, Prosecution, and Defence will all have the opportunity of considering that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how you could understand my words, that the parties were assisting the Chamber in -- they couldn't do that without having access to that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. That's very clear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no further issues to be raised at this moment, Madam Registrar, tomorrow morning at 9.00 we resume in this same courtroom. We adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there is another issue. I'm reminded very helpfully by Ms. Loukas. We're having -- we're getting -- we're being given as much help as we can, but we do have all kinds of issues always about the transmission of material between us and Mr. Krajisnik and through the UN DU and so on. The position we're faced with at the moment is we have a CD which contains material germane to tomorrow's witness, and we are unclear, and it's often very difficult for us to get clear -- we are unclear whether we are permitted to hand it to Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he's not allowed to receive it from you at this moment. But I think it could be delivered, with all the risk of falling out of baskets, et cetera. If there's any need for assistance, I'll be there to see what I can do. But I don't think that he's allowed to bring them with him himself. That has got something to do also with transportation. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the difficulty we're having, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any specific questions, I'm available and you can address Ms. Philpott.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. It's obviously urgent; it's for tomorrow's witness. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
